news.title: Donald Trump calls heckler a 'spoiled child' at Alaska rally in on-stage outburst
news.text: President Donald Trump took a heckler to task during a rally in Alaska, as part of his campaign to bolster Republican candidates ahead of the midterm elections. As the president was discussing his 2024 triumph over former Vice President Kamala Harris, a disturbance could be heard amongst the crowd. "Sounds like we have a spoiled child," he commented, prompting boos from the audience. The camera swiftly swung towards the commotion, before quickly refocusing on Trump , who commended the police. "Wow, good law enforcement!" he exclaimed. Eventually, the camera caught sight of a man being ushered out of the Curtis D. Menard Memorial Sports Center. "Wow, good job! Wow!" Trump applauded, reports the Mirror US . "He's now got the displeasure of going home to his mother and father, who both voted for me by the way," the president remarked about the heckler. This follows a similar incident just yesterday in Youngstown, where a female heckler was punched in the face by a male attendee before security intervened to escort her from the event. During the scuffle, Trump referred to the woman as a "fat guy" who needs to "go on a diet." The woman, sporting a shirt reading "Release the Epstein files," was shoved to the floor by a male participant, struck in the face, and dragged by the hair. During the attack, the president branded the woman a "paid protester" who receives cash from "the lefties in order to destroy our country. They're scum." Echoing this latest episode, Trump declared the woman would be "going back home to mom," alleging that the demonstrator's parents likely backed him. "That's a very low-class protestor," he remarked. "What he doesn't know is his mother and father voted for me. He's going to get home and he's going to get smacked." In recent days, the president has staged events in Nebraska, Texas, New York, Tennessee, and Ohio to strengthen the GOP's prospects in fiercely competitive contests. The Wasilla gathering follows a comparable rally in Fairbanks last week headlined by Vice President JD Vance. The occasions were organised to drum up backing for Alaskan Sen. Dan Sullivan, who finds himself in a tight battle that may decide whether Republicans maintain Senate control following next month's midterms. Sullivan confronts opposition from former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola, who secured more ballots than Sullivan in Alaska's open primary during August. Trump has traditionally been quite popular in Wasilla. The district backed him with over 75% of the vote in 2024. Trump clinched Alaska's presidential elections in 2016, 2020, and 2024, but recent surveys suggest his popularity in the state is on the decline.
news.summary: President Donald Trump called out a heckler while headlining a rally in Wasilla, Alaska, on Tuesday as part of his effort to boost Republican candidates ahead of the midterm elections
news.author: Cheyenne Ubiera,Peter Hennessy

news.title: Georgia Senate debate takeaways: Ossoff shoos off interest in WH bid
news.text:
For the second time in less than a week Democratic incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff aggressively jousted with Republican challenger Mike Collins, who is struggling to keep Georgia's critical U.S. Senate race competitive.

Both contenders came out swinging during the Oct. 13 encounter much like they did five days prior when they exchanged personal insults while sharing policy contrasts.

Ossoff used the forum to grill Collins about his support for unpopular parts of President Donald Trump's agenda, condemning his opponent for refusing to publicly concede who won the 2020 election results and for hiring campaign aides with a history of expressing racist and antisemitic views.

But the 39-year-old Democrat mostly pounced on how the administration's trade war has helped raise prices.

"Folks are going to the grocery store; they're paying more than ever to stock their fridge," Ossoff said.

The hourlong debate, hosted by the Atlanta Press Club, also touched on immigration, voting rights and if Democrats would impeach Trump for a third time should they retake Congress.

Ossoff entered the midterm cycle as the only Senate Democrat seeking reelection in a state Trump won in 2024, which had many political observers initially casting him as the most vulnerable Democrat in the midterm cycle.

But that narrative has faded from headlines starting with Georgia Republicans failing to recruit Gov. Brian Kemp, a popular figure, to run for the seat. Collins is trailing by as much as 13 percentage points in some polls.

Democrats are now eagerly watching the race largely over speculation that Ossoff could run for president in 2028, citing the Peach State's pivotal battleground status and rising national profile due to viral takedowns of the Trump administration.

"What Ossoff has shown in his political career by winning a seat in Georgia is that he can speak to a diverse group of voters, whether that's Democrats or Republicans, and so I think that if he wins this race, he will be considered a serious presidential contender," Rotimi Adeoye, a Democratic comms strategist, told USA TODAY in June.

Here are the key moments from Tuesday's debate:

Running for president: Ossoff pledges to serve out term

The first question didn't avoid a conversation that's been orbiting Ossoff for months — will he seek the White House in two years?

Back in August, a national poll from Emerson College showed Ossoff leading Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a hypothetical matchup.

More recent surveys have Georgia's first Jewish senator among the top five Democrats in a potential presidential primary with about 8% behind Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-New York, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris.

But when asked if he will serve a full six-year term if reelected, Ossoff expressed having "zero interest" in running for president in 2028.

"I'm running for re-election to the Senate, and tonight the contrast could not be clearer between these two Senate candidates," Ossoff said.

'I'm a little tired of this': Ossoff, Collins gets testy over racist ties

Much like during the first clash, Ossoff and Collins' exchange turned personal when the conversation focused on the Republican congressman's record of hiring campaign aides with a history of espousing anti-Black and antisemitic views.

"I condemn any sort of hate speech, anti-Semitism, hate of any kind (and) it's abhorrent," Collins said when asked if he were a white nationalist.

The GOP nominee immediately pivoted to spotlighting Ossoff's support for other Senate candidates, such as Abdul El-Sayed, of Michigan, and accused his Democratic rival of having a connection to influencer Hassan Piker, a popular left-wing activist who has become a lightning rod in the 2026 midterms for several controversial online comments.

Ossoff did not relent, however, once again mentioning that Collins' son-in-law reportedly shares neo-Nazi imagery online. He called Collins a "weak" person and asked the congressman to promise it would no longer "be produced" from his home.

In a 30-second rebuttal, Collins called out how a New York man was arrested for threatening to kill him and his son-in-law, which he said was due to Ossoff's comments. "I'm a little tired of this," he said.

Ossoff seeks to yoke Collins to Trump's trade war

Over and over again Ossoff reminded viewers how much prices have gone up and connected those costs to the Trump administration's trade war and other policy choices.

"Ground beef is up 30% since Donald Trump took office," Ossoff said. "Coffee is up 30% since Donald Trump took office, those were your votes. Tariffs you supported last week. You said the tariffs were making things fair, and I think that you should explain to Georgia voters why you voted for the tariffs and what you mean by that."

Collins, who is endorsed by Trump, at one point conceded "diesel prices are high." AAA reports the average gallon of diesel is $5.74. But the GOP congressman said, "supply is coming," slamming Ossoff for supporting mass transit and other environmental regulations.

"If it wasn't so, he wouldn't have voted for that Green New Deal. If it wasn't so, they wouldn't have killed the Keystone Pipeline," Collins said. "If it wasn't so, they'd be helping to to get us to where we're energy independent." He voted against that."

Rivals differ slightly over AI amid growing fears

The rise of artificial intelligence has unified voters with polls showing more Americans opposing than favoring construction of data centers in their areas.

Asked about the role of AI in the country's future, Ossoff called it the "most complex and important legislative question of our time." He called for federal inspectors and the fortification of the federal system in defense from bioterrorism.

"We have to recognize that we cannot allow the Trump administration, which is opposed to any regulation whatsoever, to put jobs at risk or our national security at risk," Ossoff said.

On Sept. 29 Trump convened six major technology companies who signed a joint commitment meant to self-regulate the safe development of AI.

Collins emphasized that the United States is in a race with China over the technology, which he said is already in many American's lives. He said if voters don't want data centers, he's oppose to the development, but would favor them being built if a community wanted one.

"The problem is there's a lot of bad actors out there in anything that you have," Collins said. "But before we even get there, we need to make sure that these data centers are not harming the local infrastructure, like the water and electricity."

Debate turns to election rules and 2020 denialism

Multiple times during the debate Collins was asked whether Trump prevailed in the 2020 election over former President Joe Biden.

He never answered yes or no, but instead said Biden "went into office," before adding "and boy, Georgians paid for it." Collins has falsely asserted Trump won Georgia six years ago during this campaign, including shortly before the Republican primary race.

Later, Collins expressed support for the administration's call to overhaul U.S. elections under the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act, or SAVE America Act, which stalled in the Senate this year.

The measure would have, among other things, required registered voters to present a form of approved photo identification such as a passport or driver's license before receiving a ballot.

"You know the problem is that we have voter ID here in Georgia. We do, but when offered the opportunity at least five times, Jon Ossoff voted against the SAVE Act to get voter ID for all across this country," Collins said.

"Y'all, we live in the best country in the world. There's no reason we shouldn't have the most secure elections in the world."

Ossoff responded by slamming his opponent for supporting the establishment of a fund for participants in the Jan. 6, 2021 riot at the U.S. Capitol. In August, a video showed Collins agreeing with a Georgia man who was convicted of charges stemming from the attack and who suggested that the rioters were "victims of a weaponized political system."

"Mike Collins is on record supporting handing your tax dollars to the violent thugs and criminals who sacked the U.S. Capitol and tried to overturn the election," Ossoff said.

Contributing: Jay Stahl, Irene Wright

news.title: Ice cold: Even in Alaska, Trump can’t avoid being protested at rally — breaks out more ‘your mom’ shots
news.text:
President Donald Trump can’t avoid being protested at his rallies as he campaigns for Republicans ahead of November’s midterm elections — including in red-leaning Alaska. 

Amid record-low approval ratings, Trump is attempting to fire up his base to vote for members of his party as if he were on the ballot, as he often tells them to do. But the president has faced resistance from a series of lone protesters who have interrupted his rallies in Texas, Ohio and now Alaska. 

What is Trump’s savvy retort? “Your mom” jokes. 

Shortly after Trump took the stage in Wasilla, Alaska, at around 8:30 p.m. ET on Tuesday, a protester turned heads. 

As the president was bashing his 2024 presidential opponent, former Vice President Kamala Harris, he stopped to call the demonstrator a “spoiled child.”

“Sounds like we have a spoiled child,” Trump said as his supporters booed at the protester and chanted “USA, USA, USA.” 

As the protester, wearing a sweatshirt with a picture of a bald eagle carrying an American flag on it, was being escorted out, the president commended the “good law enforcement.” 

“He’s now got the displeasure of going home to his mother and father, who both voted for me, by the way,” Trump said of the protester. 

Alaskans have voted for the Republican presidential nominee since at least 1980, according to 270toWin. Trump won the vote with 51.3 percent support in 2016, 52.8 percent in 2020 and 54.5 percent in 2024. 

Trump was in Youngstown, Ohio, last night, stumping for Sen. Jon Husted, who is running against former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown, and Vivek Ramaswamy, who ran against Trump for president in 2024 before endorsing him. Ramaswamy is running for governor in Ohio against Democrat Amy Acton, former director of the Ohio Department of Health. 

During last night’s rally, Trump gushed about how attractive and athletic Husted, a college football star, was, telling a crowd of his supporters, “I looked at his a**, and I looked at the whole, and then I looked at his hands. Look at his hands. He's got these like claws.”

During one of two protests last night, Trump said the demonstrators “get paid by the lefties in order to destroy our country. They're scum.”

He then taunted the demonstrator currently causing a commotion, saying, “He's going back home to mom...He's got to go on a diet. He's a fat guy.”

“What he doesn't know is that his mother and father voted for me,” the president added, using a similar insult that he used against a protester in San Antonio, Texas, last week. 

Wasilla was Trump’s latest stop as he vigorously campaigns in red states with the midterms right around the corner. The president is trying to boost Republican candidates’ chances as he struggles with his own image issues. 

A whopping 65 percent of Americans disapproved of Trump’s job as president, while just 32 percent approved in a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll. The Trump administration has been dogged by an unpopular war in Iran and stubborn inflation affecting Americans at the gas pump and grocery store. 

While the party in power typically loses seats in the midterm elections, recent polling shows Democrats gaining ground in Senate races in states that Republicans would normally coast through.

Mary Peltola, a former Democratic congresswoman, is beating Republican Senator Dan Sullivan by 7 percentage points, 50 to 43 percent, according to a New York Times/Siena University poll of likely voters in Alaska released earlier this month. 

Peltola led by a slimmer margin in a poll recently released by Alaska Survey Research. The Democrat was just two percentage points ahead of Sullivan, 47 to 45 percent, among Alaska’s likely voters.
news.summary: Trump fumed at a protester in Wasilla, Alaska, calling them a ‘spoiled child,’ among other insults, after they interrupted his stump speech for Republican Senate candidate Dan Sullivan
news.author: Rachel Dobkin

news.title: Donald Trump launches attack on 'spoiled child' as protester disrupts Alaska rally
news.text: Donald Trump has launched another attack at an audience member after his rally in Alaska was interrupted by a heckler. The US President has travelled to Alaska ahead of the crucial midterm elections, in the hope of drumming up more support before election day on November 3. But, all did not go as planned as he was speaking about his 2024 victory against former Vice President Kamala Harris , with an altercation taking place in the crowd, The US Mirror reports . "Sounds like we have a spoiled child," Trump said as the audience booed. The camera quickly panned over to the situation, but quickly returned to Trump, who praised the police. "Wow, good law enforcement!" he said. As he was escorted out, Trump added: “He’s now got the displeasure of going home to his mother and father who both voted for me, by the way.” It comes after a similar incident a day earlier in Youngstown, where a female heckler was punched in the face by a male attendee before security stepped in to remove her from the event. During the incident, Trump referred to the woman as a "fat guy" who needs to "go on a diet." Nearly an hour behind schedule, the president took the stage just after 4:20 p.m. local time in Wasilla. The rally is being held at a local hockey arena. On the rink, there are seats where the ice would otherwise be. Many in the crowd were seen waving American flags and “Make America Great Again” caps. The events were planned to boost support for Alaskan Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is in a heated race that could determine whether Republicans keep control of the Senate after the midterms next month. Sullivan faces a challenge from former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola, who received more votes than Sullivan did in Alaska's open primary in August. During his speech, the US President announced what he claimed was “one of the biggest deals ever made”, claiming that Taiwan will purchase gas from a natural gas project in Alaska that Senator Dan Sullivan is touting in his reelection campaign. There was no immediate confirmation from Taiwan, the self-governing island that China claims as its own. There were also no immediate further details from the White House. “Taiwan has just agreed to buy 30% of the gas coming off the pipeline for the next 20 years,” Trump said. “That guarantees success. It’s one of the biggest commitments in history for anything. It’s one of the biggest deals ever made.” Taiwan has also agreed to invest more than $4 billion in the project, Trump said. The president had similarly touted a $54 billion investment from South Korea in the Alaska pipeline, although South Korean officials had initially said the country needed to assess the project’s viability before actually committing to it.
news.summary: It comes just one day after another protester at a rally by the US President was punched in the face by a male attendee before security stepped in to remove her from the event
news.author: Cheyenne Ubiera,Peter Hennessy

news.title: Collins Spars With Jackson Over Healthcare, Campaign Finances in 3rd Maine Senate Debate
news.text:
Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson clashed over healthcare affordability, rising heating costs, and campaign financing in the third debate in the high-stakes race for Maine’s U.S. Senate seat.

Moderators opened the Oct. 13 debate by asking the candidates how they would lower heating costs after estimates suggested Mainers will spend an additional $725 this year to heat their homes compared to the previous winter.

Collins blamed Jackson’s leadership in the Maine Senate for the state’s higher heating costs and touted her work in Congress to provide access to the Low-Income Heating Assistance Program (LIHEAP).

Jackson retorted that heating oil costs have risen roughly 80 percent in Maine from last year, based on data from the state’s Department of Energy Resources. He called LIHEAP a “short-term band-aid” for Mainers struggling with increased energy costs from the Iran war.

“The biggest factor that we have right now is the Iran War, and I would get us out of the Iran War. Unlike Senator Collins, who voted five times to put us in that war, because she does whatever Donald Trump wants,” Jackson said.

Collins said she voted nine times to end the Iran war. Jackson called these votes “too late” after President Donald Trump had pushed forward with his plan and suggested the senator should have used her influence as chair of the Senate Committee on Appropriations to cut off funding to the war if she wanted it to end.

When it came to healthcare, Collins championed her bipartisan efforts to lower healthcare costs and prescription drug prices. Jackson criticized the senator for advancing Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill, which cut federal spending on Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program by $1 trillion.

Jackson said he supports Medicare for All and claimed it would fuel the economy by cutting costs for employers and allow them to hire more workers without needing to provide employee healthcare.

Collins said she would support expanding access to Medicare, but suggested the federal government needs to clean up fraud in both that program and Medicaid.

The debate heated up when Jackson derided Collins for her long list of billionaire donors, including X and Tesla CEO Elon Musk. Super political action committees (PACs) associated with Musk have donated more than $100 million to the senator’s campaign.

Collins responded by criticizing Jackson for not yet submitting a Federal Election Commission (FEC) filing and suggested the public doesn’t know who is funding the progressive Democrat’s campaign.

“He’s yet to tell us. He promised to be completely transparent, yet he has not filed a single report,” Collins said.

Jackson responded that he would release the report “tomorrow.”

“So she didn’t deny that 90 billionaires are funding her. But look, I'll give you the report tomorrow morning. How about that?” he said.

“Because we see yours, and I know that there’s no billionaires funding me. So we’ll look. I'll give you the report tomorrow, and then we’ll talk about it on Thursday,” Jackson added, referring to the candidates’ fourth and final debate on Oct. 15.

Networks WABI-TV and WAGM hosted a debate for the closely watched race on Tuesday in Bangor, bringing Collins and Jackson together onstage for a third time as the two candidates vied for Mainers’ support in the final weeks ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

Collins, 73, is seeking a sixth term in the U.S. Senate and is largely running on her track record and voting history in Congress’s upper chamber. She has highlighted her Senate tenure and chairmanship of the Senate Appropriations Committee as key assets over her opponent, a relative newcomer to national politics.

Jackson, 58, was a logger before entering the Maine Legislature and rising to state Senate president as a Democrat. A progressive, he supports Medicare for All, abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), raising lodging taxes for out-of-state visitors, expanding worker rights, and ceasing arms sales to Israel.

After failing to oust Collins in 2020 when then-candidate Joe Biden swept Maine by more than 9 percentage points, Democrats are looking for an opening this year as polls increasingly give the party a generous generic ballot advantage nationally, and as Jackson builds a small lead in polling averages.

Their second debate two days later rehashed many of these issues, with Jackson claiming that Collins and her husband were profiting off the war in Iran. Outraged, the senator told Jackson he owed her an apology, spurring Jackson to say, “No, you owe me an apology.”

The two candidates were also asked about their views on term limits in Congress. Jackson said he “absolutely” supports them as “they work well” in Maine.

Collins, now the longest-serving Republican woman in the upper chamber’s history, said she does not support term limits.

“That’s what you have elections for,” she said.

Jackson currently holds a modest 1.2-percentage-point lead over Collins in the RealClearPolitics polling average.

Out of all the states then-Vice President Kamala Harris won in 2024, Maine is the only one with a Republican senator.
news.summary: The debate heated up after Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Democrat Troy Jackson tussled over who is funding each other's campaigns.
news.author: Jacob Burg

news.title: Fact Check: Democrats Claim White House App Contains 'Spyware'
news.text:
CLAIM: Left-wing personalities and politicians have claimed the White House app contains “spyware” via “a location tracker with NO WAY to disable it.”

VERDICT: FALSE. Tech security firm NowSecure reported that its testing of the White House app found no evidence of location data being collected or transmitted.

President Donald Trump’s White House app soared to first place in the App Store’s news category as the administration launched the 24-hour “Trump TV” livestream amid the ban on certain establishment outlets from the briefing room, prompting Democrats to slander the app as location-tracking “spyware.”

CNN, MS NOW, and Politico announced last month that they were suing the president and other senior administration officials after they were denied access to the White House on September 18 as punishment for reporting “fake news,” Breitbart News reported. A federal judge issued a directive in favor of the news organizations’ lawsuit, ordering that White House access be “immediately” restored to the three outlets, though the legal dispute is still ongoing. 

Broadcasters in the White House television press pool — Fox News, ABC, CBS, NBC and CNN — temporarily halted pool coverage of the White House in a move of solidarity with the blocked outlets. 

The White House quickly launched its own official coverage on “Trump TV: The Essentials Station,” with ’round-the-clock streaming on its official app and YouTube channel. 

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) called the move an example of “authoritarianism in action” on X:

Disgraced “never-Trump” group The Lincoln Project accused the president of being a “communist.”

Progressive commentator Dean Withers said, “It’s official, we live in North Korea.”

Headquarters, formerly known as former Vice President Kamala Harris’s online campaign hub, “Kamala HQ,” also said the Trump administration’s move was “similar to Russia and North Korea.”

“America is becoming hell,” whined left-wing commentator Ed Krassenstein:

A viral post from “GOP L’s” falsely claimed the White House app “contains a location tracker with NO WAY to disable it.”

Failed New York Democrat House candidate Melanie D’Arrigo called the app “Trump administration spyware.”

In reality, the White House app has never transmitted users’ location, nor does it contain “spyware.”

Tech security firm NowSecure reported that its testing found no evidence of location data being collected or transmitted, despite the claims from left-wing personalities and politicians:

Recent reporting on the White House mobile app has overstated several security and privacy concerns by focusing on what the app could do rather than what it actually does in practice.
NowSecure analyzed the app using static and dynamic mobile application security testing. We found no evidence of unauthorized location tracking described in media coverage.
The app behaves like most modern mobile applications. It uses common third-party components and generally follows standard platform controls. It doesn’t present an unusual risk to users.
This is a good example of how easy it is to misread mobile app behavior without testing it in a real environment.

Speaking with Breitbart News White House correspondent Nick Gilbertson, White House Deputy Communications Director Kaelan Dorr responded to critics who have made up concerns about Trump TV and the app’s security. 

“There’s a lot of criticism about the safety of the app and things like that. And these are all just fake news hoaxes,” Dorr said. “Quite frankly, a lot of the technology that we use to develop these things is on par with Fortune 500 companies,” he continued, naming the NBA and Tiffany as major brands that use the same technology for their apps. 

“So, there’s nothing to be worried about,” Dorr added. “This app is incredible, and we’re going to work on integrating America.gov […] it’s about restoring the dignity of the American public, making sure everything’s in one place, you don’t have to go hunt for what you’re interested in or what you are looking for. We’re going to come to you, and it’s such a contrast with the previous administration where everyone had come begging and pleading for information about whether the president was even working at the time. They know the president’s working here.”

Olivia Rondeau is a politics reporter for Breitbart News based in Washington, DC. Find her on X/Twitter and Instagram.
news.summary:
President Donald Trump's White House application soared to first place in the App Store’s news category as the administration launched the 24-hour "Trump TV" livestream amid the ban on certain establishment outlets from the briefing room, prompting Democrats to slander the app as location-tracking "spyware."

news.title: Trump’s MAGA map scheme blows up in his face as ‘huge star’ surges: strategist
news.text:
A congressional map redrawn to hand Republicans another seat is turning on President Donald Trump, according to a strategist on the ground.

Democratic strategist Jackie Rosa, who works with the group The Bench, told host Tim Miller on Tuesday's episode of "The Bulwark Daily" that Bobby Pulido, a Tejano music star running in a South Texas district Gov. Greg Abbott redrew ahead of the midterms, now holds a commanding lead there despite Trump carrying it by 16 to 18 points.

"I believe the latest poll was 13 points up, which is pretty crazy," Rosa said.

Rosa, whose father's side of the family has lived in the Rio Grande Valley "since before Texas was a state," said there was plenty of doubt last year that anyone could flip a district like it.

"This is one of the most swingy, swingiest areas in the country. People are not beholden to a party. It's very much the candidate," she said. "And someone like Bobby is very much in alignment with the people there culturally, values-wise."

Pulido, the son of Tejano music pioneer Roberto Pulido, was born and raised in South Texas and still lives there. Rosa said his family's music has been "the soundtrack of South Texas life" at weddings, baptisms and carne asadas for decades.

"Bobby's very famous in his own right and is a huge star," Rosa said. "Obviously you see a lot of celebrities run for office...With Bobby, it's very different because it's so cultural."

Rosa pointed to a recent rally in Beeville, a small town in a rural South Texas county that she called "ruby red," where Pulido appeared alongside gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa and Senate candidate James Talarico. She said nearly 3,000 people turned out.

"More people showed up at this rally than the entire county voted for Kamala Harris in 2024," Rosa said.

She added that the region's 2024 swing toward Trump came as residents "felt neglected" over the border and the economy, but said the Trump administration's immigration raids have since hit the Valley hard.

"What's happening right now is just not humane. It's not sustainable," Rosa said. "[It] is also destroying the economy there."

news.title: Battle lines shift in House races as Republicans retreat from front-line districts
news.text:
DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — Republicans were retreating Tuesday from a handful of battleground U.S. House races while Democrats were racing to raise money to boost candidates who seemed like long shots earlier this year.

The Congressional Leadership Fund, the leading House Republican super PAC, canceled spending in four races from the Midwest to the East Coast and increased its investment in 16 other races from Texas to Pennsylvania. Another super PAC allied with President Donald Trump is cutting back in a battleground district in the Las Vegas area. 

The decisions were disclosed by three Republican campaign officials familiar with the plans who spoke on condition of anonymity to share private strategy conversations. 

Meanwhile, Democrats' House campaign committee is eyeing openings in Republican-held districts and hoping to raise millions of dollars in the next week to fuel a late round of advertising that they say could net at least a half dozen more seats. 

The shifting money in the final three weeks of midterm campaigns points to an increasingly defensive posture by Republicans, who have already trimmed their expectations in U.S. Senate races, and new aggression from Democrats, who are trying to capitalize on President Donald Trump's weak approval ratings.

“You can tell now where people are competing based on where they’re putting the money,” said Stu Sandler, a Republican strategist working on House and statewide races this year.

David McIntosh, president of the conservative Club For Growth, said there are only a few places where Republicans could pick up seats this year. 

"The economic environment has not been good," he said. “Voters are dissatisfied with their Republican majority and the base is also dissatisfied with that they weren’t able to get the SAVE America Act passed,” referring to Trump's plan for a strict proof-of-citizenship voting bill.

“It looked like Republicans were weak,” McIntosh said, “and so you’ve seen a lot of drop-off in enthusiasm.”

Republicans cut back in front-line districts

The Congressional Leadership Fund is no longer spending on advertising in Iowa's 1st District, where three-term Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks is defending her seat against Democrat Christina Bohannan.

Bohannan is running for her third time against Miller-Meeks. Last time, the race was decided by only 799 votes, making it the second-closest in the country. It's an eastern Iowa district where congressional cuts to Medicaid have been linked to hospital service closures and high diesel prices have been a challenge for farmers. 

Likewise, the officials said the group won't keep spending in New Jersey's 7th District, where second-term Republican Rep. Tom Kean is facing off against Democrat Rebecca Bennett. Kean has been under scrutiny for his four-month absence from Congress, which he left unexplained until disclosing a mental health crisis upon his return. Kean, who won by 5.4 percentage points two years ago, has also faced questions over his support for Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war.

These races, as well as one in the Cincinnati, Ohio, area and one in east-central Michigan, have accounted for $13.3 million in Congressional Leadership Fund spending, more than 12% of its total through Oct. 13. 

The group will instead reinforce districts where Trump beat Democrat Kamala Harris by narrow margins in 2024. 

Safety and Affordability, an offshoot of MAGA Inc., pulled nearly $1 million in ad spending aimed at helping Republican Marty O’Donnell’s campaign in Nevada’s 3rd District. Republicans had hoped that Trump's tax-cut legislation — specifically no taxes on tips — would resonate in Las Vegas and help defeat Democratic Rep. Susie Lee, who voted against the bill.

Sandler said his party needs to turn out voters who usually participate in presidential elections but often stay home in the midterms.

“One thing you can’t say is that they’ve been under-resourced,” he said. “Republican resources are at a high. They’ve never been this well-funded in the midterm.”

Democrats try to scrounge up more money

As House Republicans have retrenched, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee believes at least a dozen more races could be within striking distance. However, they need more money to take advantage. 

The committee launched a $17 million fundraising drive, with a deadline of Oct. 22, to pump advertising onto the air in districts that were once seen as out of reach.

“It’s not that we need the money to win in the districts where we have been running to get to 218 seats,” said Courtney Rice, the committee’s communication director. “We’re talking about the next level.” 

One is Ohio's 10th, a Dayton-area district represented by 12-term Republican Rep. Mike Turner. Democrats see Turner as beatable despite the former Dayton mayor's durability and 18 percentage-point victory two years ago. Trump carried the district by six percentage points in 2024.

Turner didn't begin advertising until late September, according to AdImpact, later than most competitive House incumbents, and the National Republican Congressional Committee started spending there this week.

If the Democratic committee reaches its goal, it would also start spending in the Miami area, suburban St. Louis, Missouri and the Little Rock, Arkansas, area. They would be able to buy ads in coordination with the campaigns at the lower rate available to candidates, due to a June Supreme Court decision, squeezing more ad time from those dollars. 

Nebraska sees surge of spending 

Senate Republicans are pouring millions more into Nebraska to protect Sen. Pete Ricketts, the latest sign of how dramatically their spending priorities have shifted from battleground states toward defending seats they once expected to hold comfortably.

Ricketts is facing a challenge from independent Dan Osborn, who is backed by Democrats. Trump won Nebraska by more than 20 percentage points in 2024.

The Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Senate GOP leadership, said Tuesday it was behind a $15 million investment in the state.

Other groups are also pumping money into the race, with the cryptocurrency-backed super PAC Fairshake launching a $7 million advertising campaign, according to AdImpact data. 

The group has also increased its investment in Ohio’s Senate race, bringing its total spending there to $45 million in support of Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who is up against Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown. 

The Nebraska investment follows new spending by the Senate Leadership Fund in Kansas and South Carolina, two other states Trump won by double digits in 2024. All three were absent from the group’s initial $342 million advertising plan in April, which has since been reshaped as Republicans pulled back from Georgia and North Carolina, two states that were central to their original strategy.

Democrats are also shifting their resources. The Senate Democrats’ main spending arm said Tuesday it was pulling its advertising last week from Georgia, where Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has built a substantial fundraising advantage over Republican Rep. Mike Collins, and focusing instead on Maine, New Hampshire, Michigan, Iowa, Kansas, Texas, Alaska and Ohio.

The shifting investments come as both parties make their final spending decisions in the battle for Senate control, with Democrats pointing to their candidates and the political environment as potential counterweights to Republican money.

In a letter to fellow senators Tuesday, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said the battle for control of the chamber “comes down to one defining question.”

“Will the unprecedented tsunami of Republican money defeat the massive Democratic advantage in candidates, policies, and political climate?” Schumer asked.

news.title: An AI image of Mia Goth sparks Instagram fan account controversy
news.text:
AI-generated images can now give celebrities entire social media moments they never took part in. For Mia Goth, that meant a supposed response to her divorce — right down to a T-shirt and breakup soundtrack.After news of the Pearl and MaXXXine actress's divorce filing from Shia LaBeouf a few weeks ago, an Instagram post appeared to show Goth wearing a shirt that read "MY EX IS MY BIGGEST FAN." Paired with Beyoncé’s "Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It)," it was easy to read as a comment on the split.Except Goth’s representative says the image was AI-generated. And Goth doesn’t even use social media.The post came from @miagoth_, a verified fan account with more than a million followers. Despite the fan-page label, People initially wrote about the image as a selfie Goth had posted herself, describing the shirt as her fashion choice days after filing for divorce. (The article and post have both been removed.) 

 Taylor Swift's wedding photos are going viral. There's just one problem.

That confusion is exactly what the actress's team says it has been trying to stop."Mia Goth does not have ownership of, nor does she engage in social media on any platform," her representative, Christine Tripicchio, told The Verge. "We have filed multiple complaints with Instagram to remove the verified fan account which continues to post counterfeit, AI images of Mia Goth."Tripicchio also questioned how the account had qualified for a verification badge in the first place."The fact that this fan account meets Instagram’s criteria to qualify for a 'blue check' is disconcerting on a fundamental level," she said. "Beyond that, it is incomprehensible that Instagram evidently prioritizes the dissemination of forged and manipulated images over the protection and integrity of a public figure’s likeness."In response, Meta told Mashable, "This account has been removed for impersonating a public figure.""We must call out the misuse of AI"Goth’s team isn’t alone in trying to correct a public moment that never happened.A March investigation by Indicator identified six AI-generated influencer accounts with roughly a million Instagram followers combined that posted fabricated celebrity encounters. One, @ayannasoblack, shared fake gym photos with Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson and John Cena. All but one of the accounts linked to Fanvue profiles selling access to synthetic adult content.Real performers' work also supplies material for these accounts. As Mashable reported, AI personas have recently reproduced comedians' jokes and performances to build audiences. Comedian Sarah Purdum told Mashable that women’s material was being "stolen and repurposed for sexy AI models."

 Fake influencers, real money: Inside the AI creator business

For celebrities, the consequences extend beyond invented encounters. In January 2024, nonconsensual, sexually explicit AI-generated images of Taylor Swift spread online, prompting SAG-AFTRA to condemn them as "upsetting, harmful, and deeply concerning." Later that year, Swift cited a separate fabrication — images falsely suggesting she supported Donald Trump — when announcing her endorsement of Kamala Harris."It really conjured up my fears around AI, and the dangers of spreading misinformation," she wrote.Scarlett Johansson raised a similar objection in 2025 after an AI-generated video depicted her and other Jewish celebrities protesting Ye’s antisemitism. Although she condemned antisemitism, she objected to being included in a video she never participated in. "We must call out the misuse of AI, no matter its messaging, or we risk losing a hold on reality," she said in a statement.Even deceased performers' families are being left to push back: In October 2025, filmmaker Zelda Williams asked people to stop sending her AI-generated videos of her father, Robin Williams, saying the recreations were "NOT what he’d want."What is Instagram's current AI policy?An image being AI-generated doesn’t automatically mean Meta will take it down.In its explanation of its policy, Meta says it generally keeps manipulated content available unless it breaks another platform rule, such as those against bullying or harassment. Instead, it uses "AI info" labels to provide context when it detects certain technical signals or someone discloses AI use.

 Meta leans into AI in your feeds

Even those labels have needed adjusting, though. In 2024, Meta changed "Made with AI" to "AI info" after acknowledging that some photos with minor AI retouching were getting flagged. It later moved labels for content detected as AI-edited into the post’s menu, while keeping visible labels on content detected as AI-generated.But that approach depends on detecting AI use in the first place. Meta has acknowledged that its systems can’t identify every AI-generated image and that the invisible markers it uses for detection can be removed. A missing AI label doesn't necessarily mean a photo is real (clearly).
news.summary: Mia Goth’s team says a verified Instagram fan account posted AI-generated images of her, raising questions about celebrity likenesses and Meta’s rules.

news.title: Alaska Could Elect Its First Democratic Governor in Decades
news.text: Alaska voters might elect a Democratic governor for the first time since 1998 as polls show Democrat Jonathan Kreiss‑Tomkins maintaining an impressive lead over his three Republican opponents. Alaska has not had a Democratic governor since Tony Knowles left office in 2002 and the state have opted for Republican candidates in every presidential election since 1968, with President Donald Trump carrying it by double digits in 2016, 2020 and 2024. Trump received 54.5 percent of the vote in 2024, a 13.1-point lead over former Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris. But voters in the Last Frontier have historically shown a willingness to split their political tickets. Democrat Mark Begich was elected to the Senate in 2008, and voters elected Democrat Mary Peltola to the House in 2022. Peltola is now running for Senate. This year, Democrats are hopeful that voters might opt for a Democratic governor in a race that has become unexpectedly competitive. There are four candidates for Alaska governor, including three Republicans: Bernadette Wilson, Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor. Kreiss-Tomkins is the lone Democrat. Four recent polls conducted since September and tracked by the New York Times show Kreiss-Tomkins leading in all. The election comes as Republicans fight to maintain control in the U.S. House and Senate amid falling approval ratings for Trump and rising concerns over the U.S. economy, including inflation, gas prices and more. While a Democratic governor in Alaska would not affect the congressional split, it could act as a warning sign for Republicans. This year's political climate has led to competitive races in states that have previously backed Republicans, including Alaska and Iowa. In Alaska, that might mean the first Democratic governor since 2002. Iowa and Alaska face the greatest odds of flipping the governor's seat to a Democrat, The Cook Political Report said in an article published Tuesday. Cook also analyzed several recent polls that found Kreiss-Tomkins leading, several times by double digits. The report is still ranking the Alaska governor seat as a Toss-Up to Lean Democrat. While Kreiss-Tomkins is polling well ahead of his Republican opponents, Cook reported that the final votes will likely be much closer than the polls indicate. How 2026 Governor Races Are Leaning Alaska is not the only gubernatorial race leaning Democratic this year, according to Cook, which assessed all governor elections in the U.S. Thirteen states are ranked as Solid Democrat, five as Lean Democrat, four as Toss-Ups, three as Lean Republican, four as Likely Republican and seven as Solid Republican. The breakdown is as follows: Democratic Chances in Alaska Senate Race Alaska voters also appear to be leaning toward a Democratic candidate in the Senate race, where Peltola is competing against Republican Dan Sullivan. A New York Times summary of recent polls finds Peltola leading Sullivan in three since late September. Earlier this month, Sabato's Crystal Ball, based out of the University of Virginia's Center for Politics, moved the Alaska race to "Leans Democratic" from its previous "Toss-Up" ranking. A Peltola victory would mark the first time in almost 20 years that Alaska has elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate. What Happens Next As early voting begins and the midterms loom ever closer, polling and reports will closely watch for signs of whether a Democrat will secure the gubernatorial seat in a state that has elected Republicans since 2002 and far longer for presidential elections. If Kreiss-Tomkins were to win, the result could reshape Alaska's political landscape only two years before the next presidential election.
