news.title: ‘To me, it’s Mohammed’: Abdul El-Sayed faces Muslim Brotherhood claims in Michigan Senate race
news.text: Three times, Abdul El-Sayed answered "no" when asked in an interview whether he or his family had ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. But on Monday, just one day after his appearance on NBC's "Meet the Press," a social media post written by his half-sister 14 years ago began circulating: Their mother, she wrote, had been active in the Islamist movement in Egypt during the 1970s, before immigrating to the United States. For El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for a U.S. Senate seat in Michigan who hopes to become the first Muslim senator in American history, the revelation is politically explosive just three weeks before the midterm elections. His Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, has already turned the posts into a campaign advertisement in a race that could determine whether Republicans retain control of the Senate or Democrats take it over for the remainder of Donald Trump's presidency. "I had an amazing conversation with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood in the early 1970s, when she was in college," Eman Abdelhadi, now a researcher at the University of Chicago, wrote on Twitter, now X, in 2012, adding the hashtag "#respect." In another post, she wrote: "My family has long been MB," referring to the Muslim Brotherhood, although she added that she believed the movement had handled politics poorly and destructively. In 2013, she wrote that relatives had been imprisoned because of their membership in the Islamist organization and asked followers to pray for family members who supported it in Egypt. Abdelhadi and El-Sayed share the same mother, Fatten Elkomy, but grew up in separate households after their parents divorced. The posts do not establish what exactly their mother did within the movement, whether her son knew about her involvement or whether he himself had any connection to the organization. The posts surfaced after El-Sayed was interviewed on NBC on Sunday and explicitly asked whether he or his family had any ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, the Islamist movement founded in Egypt from which Hamas also emerged. The question came against the backdrop of Republican efforts in recent weeks to portray him as a "radical jihadist" with links to Islamist organizations, allegations he has repeatedly denied. When moderator Kristen Welker asked whether he or his family had ties to the Brotherhood, El-Sayed replied: "No, but let's talk about this." "No, you don't have any ties?" Welker pressed. "No," he answered. "And your family doesn't?" "No," El-Sayed repeated. He argued that Rogers was raising the issue merely to repeatedly emphasize the word "Muslim" and encourage voters to view him with suspicion because of his name and religion. On Monday, Rogers circulated a new campaign video combining El-Sayed's denials from the interview with his sister's posts, accusing his opponent of lying. El-Sayed's campaign responded that Rogers was using "bad faith attacks on Abdul's faith and family" to divert attention from the cost of living and soaring gasoline and grocery prices. The campaign also maintained that allegations linking El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood had been "debunked as racist and untrue," but did not address the specific post in which his sister described their mother's involvement in the movement. The same half-sister had already caused difficulties for El-Sayed over the summer, after other old social media posts surfaced, including one described as celebrating the October 7 massacre. Support for Mohamed Morsi and indictment of organization where his mother worked El-Sayed, a prominent figure on the Democratic Party's far left and an outspoken critic of Israel, has repeatedly denied ties to extremist organizations. His critics, however, argue that his conduct raises questions about his actual beliefs. Fox News, for example, noted that on the second anniversary of the October 7 attack, El-Sayed sent an email to supporters asking them to donate money to Palestinians. In the message, he compared Hamas to the Israeli government, although he described both as "evil." The network also pointed to his campaign appearances alongside streamer Hasan Piker, who previously declared that the United States "deserved 9/11." El-Sayed described the remark as "stupid" but refused to distance himself from Piker. Although several media outlets, including the conservative Fox News, reported that they had been unable to identify any direct ties between El-Sayed and the Muslim Brotherhood, attention is now focusing on his mother's possible connection to the movement. The Brotherhood is designated a terrorist organization by several countries, including Egypt. The United States has also designated its Egyptian and Jordanian branches as terrorist organizations over their support for Hamas. The activism attributed to El-Sayed's mother by his sister dates back more than 50 years, before Hamas was founded. However, after moving to the United States, Elkomy worked for an Islamic aid organization that the U.S. government sanctioned in 2004 for supporting al-Qaeda and Hamas. According to American media reports, Elkomy worked for the Islamic American Relief Agency, or IARA. U.S. Treasury Department documents stated that the organization was responsible for transferring funds to Palestinian territories for terrorist activities and, in particular, served as a conduit for money intended for Hamas through a Western European country. In 2007, the organization was indicted. Elkomy was mentioned at least 12 times in the accompanying list of exhibits, although she herself was never charged. The exhibits documented her involvement in financial transfers and recordings of telephone conversations between 1999 and 2002. At the time, Elkomy denied that the organization had any ties to terrorism. In a 2004 interview with the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, she explained that her work involved helping orphans and children who had lost at least one parent, adding that it broke her heart to think they would no longer receive assistance. El-Sayed himself expressed support in 2011 for the revolution then unfolding in Egypt against President Hosni Mubarak. In an opinion article, he called on the United States to support the protesters even if doing so resulted in the Muslim Brotherhood coming to power. He argued that even in that scenario, there were several reasons why the resulting state would look nothing like Iran. In addition, a 2012 document published in an Egyptian newspaper listed a "Dr. Abdel-Rahman El-Sayed" from New York among its signatories. The signatories expressed support for decisions by Egypt's then-president Mohamed Morsi, a Muslim Brotherhood figure, after he expanded his presidential powers. They also called for a "purge" of the media and police. El-Sayed's campaign declined to comment on the letter. The U.S. midterm elections, scheduled for November 3, will determine control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, which are currently controlled by Republicans. Midterm elections have historically been viewed as a referendum on the sitting president, and polling has suggested that Democrats have an opportunity to take control of both chambers amid Trump's low popularity and widespread frustration with the cost of living and the sharp rise in prices caused by the war with Iran. In the Senate, where Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority, a Democratic takeover would depend heavily on the party's ability to retain its Michigan seat, which is being vacated by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. The contest between El-Sayed and Rogers is therefore considered particularly important. Polls have consistently shown El-Sayed ahead, but only by a narrow margin. El-Sayed, 41, was born to Egyptian immigrant parents. He is a medical doctor and epidemiologist who previously headed the Wayne County Department of Health Services in Michigan. He has never held elected office, although he ran for Michigan governor in 2018 and lost the Democratic primary to Gretchen Whitmer, who went on to become governor. He is considered a member of the Democratic Party's far-left progressive wing. Alongside repeated accusations that Israel committed "genocide" in Gaza, he has called for an end to all U.S. military assistance to Israel, including support for defensive systems. He argues that the money should instead be invested in American communities. In August, El-Sayed won the Democratic Senate nomination after an especially contentious primary, narrowly defeating Haley Stevens, a moderate, pro-Israel Democrat, by about one percentage point. The contest between El-Sayed and Stevens was widely regarded as a crucial test of the direction of the Democratic Party as a whole. It followed a series of victories this year by progressive candidates challenging the party's established leadership and taking strongly anti-Israel positions in local congressional and mayoral races. Those victories signaled a dramatic increase in the progressive movement's influence. Most of those successes, however, came in liberal strongholds such as New York and California, where Democratic candidates are often effectively assured of victory. Michigan, by contrast, is a swing state that Trump won in 2024 by a narrow 1.4 percentage points. For progressives, the Senate contest offers an opportunity to demonstrate that they can attract broader public support beyond their traditional strongholds. ‘Bin Laden jersey’ and the Israel-Iran comparison: ‘Both are dangerous’ Republicans, meanwhile, see Michigan as one of their best opportunities to capture a Democratic Senate seat and improve their chances of retaining control of the chamber. Against that backdrop, Trump and his allies have intensified their attacks on El-Sayed in recent days, portraying him as a dangerous extremist. Trump has repeatedly referred to the candidate as "Mohammed," even though his name is Abdul, behavior that the president's critics describe as blatant Islamophobia. In one recent social media post, Trump called him "Mohammed El-Sayed," a "RADICAL Extremist" and a "Terrorist Sympathizer." At a rally Saturday, Trump again described El-Sayed as a "radical jihadist" and explained why he had decided to call him Mohammed. "Somebody said, his name isn't Mohammed it's Abdul. I said, to me, it's Mohammed," Trump told the crowd. He added that, as president, he could call the candidate whatever he wanted, and repeated his accusation that El-Sayed was a jihadist. Trump also shared a photograph of himself and first lady Melania Trump alongside a photograph of El-Sayed and his wife, who wears a hijab, with the caption "Two VERY DIFFERENT Americas." Republican Sen. John Kennedy, who is not related to the family of the late President John F. Kennedy, appeared alongside Rogers and said that El-Sayed "sleeps in a Bin Laden jersey." On Monday, Trump shared a video in which singer Kid Rock warned of a "civil war over religious ideology" and described El-Sayed as a "wolf in sheep's clothing." El-Sayed, for his part, argues that Trump is trying to divert attention from the cost of living. "He knows my name is Abdul. He says it every day," El-Sayed responded. "But he's not just attacking me. He's attacking all of us." He accused Trump of looking down on ordinary Americans and believing that he could use El-Sayed's name and religion to distract voters from the economic hardship caused by his policies. El-Sayed said that hardship was being felt at gas stations, grocery stores and doctors' offices, and that Trump underestimated voters' ability to recognize what was happening. "It's time for change," he concluded. Even without the attacks on his identity, El-Sayed continues to generate controversy over his positions toward Israel. During a debate last week, the moderator asked him which country posed a greater danger to the United States, Israel or Iran. El-Sayed refused to choose. "I think both of them have proven dangerous in their own way," he said. He argued that Iran presented a risk of attacking the United States, while Israel was drawing Washington into wars it had no reason to fight. El-Sayed accused Israel of pushing Washington into the war with Iran. Asked whether he would support supplying defensive weapons to Israel if Iran attacked it, he rejected the idea. "I don't want our tax dollars buying weapons for other countries," he said, reiterating that he wanted public money invested in schools and health care in Michigan. Rogers responded that he would approve such assistance. The March attack on Temple Israel synagogue near Detroit has also continued to trouble El-Sayed's campaign. The attacker, who had lost relatives in an Israeli strike in Lebanon, rammed his vehicle into the synagogue building while children were inside and opened fire at a security guard. Although El-Sayed condemned the attack, he also said that "hurt people hurt people." Members of the Jewish community interpreted the remark as an attempt to justify an antisemitic terrorist attack. In August, El-Sayed apologized to the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus, saying that the timing of his remarks had been wrong. His efforts to improve relations with Jewish voters may be having some success. A group called "Jews for Abdul" has been established to help him win the election. This week, the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC also returned to the campaign. An organization affiliated with the group sent election materials opposing El-Sayed to approximately 130,000 Jewish voters in Michigan. During the Democratic primary, the lobby spent approximately $30 million supporting his more moderate opponent, Stevens, who ultimately lost. El-Sayed attacked Obama, who is now campaigning for him El-Sayed received support during the Democratic primary from prominent progressive leaders, including Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. In the final stretch of the campaign, however, he is also working to secure support from the Democratic Party's more moderate establishment, possibly in an effort to attract undecided voters. Former Vice President Kamala Harris recently appeared alongside him at an event in Detroit, and former President Barack Obama is expected to join him at a rally in the city next weekend. That support comes despite El-Sayed's past criticism of Obama. Fourteen years ago, El-Sayed, whose charismatic style has led some to call him the "Obama of Michigan," accused the then-president of perpetuating wars and undermining civil rights. During Sunday's NBC interview, El-Sayed explained that he had been "young and angry" at the time and had not understood how difficult it was to bring about meaningful change. When interviewer Kristen Welker asked whether America was ready for a Muslim president, he brought the conversation back to Michigan. "I think Michigan is ready for a Muslim senator," he said.
news.summary: The progressive Democrat holds a narrow lead over Republican Mike Rogers and hopes to become the first Muslim US senator, but resurfaced posts by his half-sister about their mother's past activism have intensified the controversy surrounding his campaign
news.author: Daniel Edelson, New York

news.title: Trump’s Genocidal Rhetoric on Iran Deserves Legal Consequences, Scholars Say
news.text:
US President Donald Trump’s threats to destroy Iran have become so frequent that they often don’t make headlines. One recent exception, though, was during his 38-minute speech at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly on September 22, in which Trump mentioned Iran 17 times.

“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before? Maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East, or even the world,” he blustered. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”

Using a mix of warnings and expletives to address Iranians, Trump falsely claimed that Tehran had refused to negotiate an agreement over its nuclear program. On both occasions when Iran was militarily attacked, in June 2025 and February 2026, it was in the middle of diplomatic talks with Trump’s envoys.

“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he added during his speech at the international organization founded in 1945 to preserve global peace and security.

The U.S. military operations in Iran, an extension of the U.S.-Israeli aggression launched in February, have largely been on hold for the past few weeks as American voters gear up for the midterm elections in less than a month — with the unpopular war remaining a hot-button issue. But White House officials have sought to preserve momentum for the conflict through continued combative rhetoric, and Trump has led the charge with occasional social media outbursts and inflammatory monologues.

The UN address is far from the only time that Trump had resorted to annihilatory language to describe his intentions with Iran. “I have a big decision coming up,” Trump told Axios earlier in September. “Do I want to go in and annihilate them, or do I not?”

“My question is, if and when I want to destroy the entire country, when do I do it?” he told Fox News days after his speech at the UN. In October, TIME published an interview in which the publication asked him to clarify his annihilation comments. “Yeah, I would do that. It’s possible.… Because by annihilating Iran, we’ve created peace in the world. With Iran, I don’t think you could ever have peace.”

Most notably, in a widely criticized Truth Social post on April 7, he wrote, “a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again,” prompting calls from several members of the Congress for his impeachment under the 25th Amendment to the Constitution, including Rep. Steve Cohen (D-Tennessee), Rep. John Garamendi (D-California), and Rep. Jan Schakowsky (D-Illinois).

Different sections of the amendment have been invoked in the past when the sitting presidents were incapable of discharging their duties. For example, on November 19, 2021, former President Joe Biden invoked Section 3 of the 25th Amendment to undergo a medical surgery and his vice president Kamala Harris took charge as acting president for 85 minutes. Still, the fourth section of the amendment laying out the authority of the vice president and cabinet members to remove the president has never been invoked.

On April 30, a group of 30 psychiatrists and psychologists published a statement declaring that Trump was contending with a serious mental health impairment. The statement, which was entered into the Congressional Record by Senators Sheldon Whitehouse and Jack Reed of Rhode Island, argued that if the signatories were called to adjudicate the president’s fitness to fulfill the obligations of his office, they would confirm that “he lacks the capacity to do so.” Still, that option has not been raised by Vice President JD Vance or members of Trump’s cabinet.

“Trump’s statement was certainly genocidal in character, in the sense that it appears to demonstrate the intent to destroy the Iranian people as a protected national group, in whole or in part,” said Heidi Matthews, an assistant professor of law at York University in Toronto, referencing the U.S. president’s chilling Truth Social post.

“Direct and public incitement to genocide is considered an ‘other genocidal act,’ in that it is a crime independent of whether or not genocide is actually carried out,” she told Truthout.

Matthews, who is also the co-director of York University’s International and Transnational Law Intensive Program, believes the legal framework to interpret these remarks has already been established: “It is certainly reasonable to consider this statement both in terms of the crime of incitement to genocide, and also as constituting an unlawful breach of Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, which prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state.”

Meanwhile, some Iranians listening to Trump’s remarks while grappling with the consequences of his aggression are concerned that the most powerful leader in the world may follow through on his rhetoric and take actions with irreversible consequences. The United States possesses nearly 5,000 nuclear warheads, and the decision to use them rests with the president.

Yalda Hasheminezhad, a 42-year-old cartoonist from Ardabil in northwestern Iran, said her reaction to Trump’s threats was a mixture of “sorrow and disbelief.”

“As a human being and as an artist, I cannot tolerate this much injustice, oppression, and violence,” Hasheminezhad told Truthout. “Behind each killing, there’s a human being, there’s a life, there’s a family, and it’s impossible to be indifferent to it.”

“I hope that one day, instead of making decisions on how to annihilate each other, people decide to live and try to make each other’s lives more peaceful. Yet, I feel that Trump isn’t a stable person and acts like a child who easily forgets what he said a few minutes ago,” she added.

In addition to his graphic comments, in recent months Trump has consistently expressed contempt for Iranians and used his Truth Social platform to publish AI-generated visuals depicting violence across Iran, including the critical Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf, which he has vowed on multiple occasions to destroy.

In one Truth Social post on September 6, he portrayed himself wielding a sledgehammer, shattering a sandstone-like map of Iran. Trump has also regularly threatened to attack civilian infrastructure; civilian sites were openly targeted during the height of U.S.-Israeli attacks.

Still, Trump’s public gestures toward Iran have been mercurial. After the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding was signed by Tehran and Washington on June 17, Trump temporarily shifted his rhetoric and praised the Iranian leadership as “very rational people” who were “nice to deal with.” At a White House dinner on June 25, he promised American farmers that they’d be able to sell their products to “the lovely country of Iran.” Once the ceasefire agreement collapsed, he went back to his more violent language.

Many international leaders have shrugged off Trump’s rhetoric. In September, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney downplayed Trump’s threat to “annihilate” Iran as speaking the “language of war.” But legal scholars specializing in the study of mass atrocities disagree, arguing that incitement to violence, even if not carried out, has been deemed criminal under international law.

“I do not think that dismissing these remarks as simply the language of war is either accurate or helpful,” said Craig Martin, co-director of the International and Comparative Law Center at Washburn University School of Law.

“These statements were clearly threats designed to coerce Iran into conceding, and they threatened actions that would have been unlawful under international law … the threats themselves may have been unlawful and even risen to the level of constituting a war crime,” he told Truthout.

Since the beginning of the war, Trump has made four international trips and met several foreign dignitaries, including at the 36th NATO Summit in Ankara in July. Throughout this time, his counterparts have rarely criticized his frightening statements. Scholars of international law believe world leaders should call out the harm of Trump’s rhetoric and align their foreign policy with their international legal obligations.

“Third states are legally obligated to ensure respect for the rules of international humanitarian law and to prevent genocide, making it imperative that leaders recognize Trump’s threats for what they are: unlawful and potentially criminal,” York University’s Matthews said, pointing to discursive double standards in safeguarding international law, which are making illegal wars more frequent.

Since September, when a United Nations fact-finding mission found reasonable grounds to believe the United States has committed war crimes in Iran by targeting civilian sites, specifically an elementary school in Minab killing more than 120 children and a sports hall in Lamerd, the question of accountability has been debated more widely.

This comes at a time when the U.S. State Department has sanctioned the International Criminal Court and clarified its determination to “dismantle” the UN-affiliated judicial system in a bid to avert future legal proceedings implicating members of the current administration and Israeli officials.

“Neither the U.S. nor Iran have ratified the Rome Statute for the International Criminal Court, but Trump could theoretically be prosecuted by another state under the well-established doctrine of universal jurisdiction,” said Marjorie Cohn, professor emerita at Thomas Jefferson School of Law and former president of the National Lawyers Guild.

“Another state could also file a case with the International Court of Justice, asking for an advisory opinion about Trump’s war crimes and genocidal threats against Iran,” she told Truthout.

But the structures of international law continue to determine the context of relations between countries, even if they have been increasingly weakened. The United Nations General Assembly remains the largest global forum for consensus-building on key issues, the Security Council makes decisions directly affecting global peace and security, and the UN’s humanitarian agencies are facilitating critical aid to war- and poverty-stricken regions.

Gabor Rona, a professor of practice at the Cardozo Law School in New York, says the bodies of international law known as jus ad bellum and jus in bello, which dictate why and how wars should be fought, are being overlooked. Still, these laws have been enshrined in the UN Charter and remain binding.

“It is forbidden to target civilians, civilian infrastructure, cultural property, hospitals, and to cause long-term and widespread environmental damage,” Rona told Truthout. “Trump’s threats violate jus ad bellum and constitute a threat to violate jus in bello. These are the types of international crimes for which Nazi leaders were prosecuted at Nuremberg.”

“Despite ongoing serious problems and conflicts, the past 80 years have seen unprecedented advances in peace, diplomacy, human development, health, welfare, education, life expectancy, etc. These advances are in no small part a product of the post-World War II international order that is now at grave risk,” he added.

Trump has suggested that he will likely resume his bombing operations in Iran after the midterms. He also rejected a new diplomatic proposal by the Iranian delegation visiting New York for the UN General Assembly and doesn’t appear to have a clear vision of why he is continuing the war. Many Iranians are adjusting to the new reality of uncertainty and violence, and some of them are ignoring his bombast.

“When I first heard him [Trump] saying a few months ago that he would do something annihilatory, I was truly scared, because we were in the middle of the war, and I was seeing he was striking different places and people were rushing to the north,” said Shabnam Assad, a 40-year-old civil engineer in Rasht.

“But over time, I saw that he’s a capricious person and changes his mind a lot, and generally, both I and many people I know have really stopped following the news. We don’t believe in anything anymore, and are simply coping with the economy,” she told Truthout. “I have concluded that I should not waste my life and time on things like this.”
news.summary: As Trump repeats annihilation threats against Iran, legal scholars implore other countries to step in.
news.author: Kourosh Ziabari

news.title: Could Iran target the Gulf’s digital backbone? The risks to data centres and internet cables explained
news.text:
The Gulf has invested billions of dollars in artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital infrastructure. But a warning from Iran has raised questions about how secure these ambitions would be if conflict with the United States resumes. Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei told Al Jazeera that the data centres, artificial intelligence facilities, and communication cables in the area could be attacked if hostility resumes.This is after the drone attack on the AWS facility in the UAE and Bahrain when the US-Israel was attacking Iran, reported by Al Jazeera.Also Read | Saudi Arabia spends $83 billion on defence. Why are missiles and drones still getting through?The concern extends beyond individual technology companies. The Gulf’s digital economy depends on undersea cables, reliable electricity and large computing facilities that can be difficult to protect during a conflict.Why the Gulf’s internet cables are vulnerableMost of the data that moves between Europe and Asia moves via fibre-optic cables laid under the ocean. The cables contain data related to business transactions, cloud computing services, and even normal Internet browsing.Live EventsAl Jazeera reports that, according to estimates provided by research firm TeleGeography, more than 90 per cent of data capacity between Europe and Asia travels via cables that go through the Red Sea. Most of the cables pass through Bab al-Mandeb, which is a narrow strip of water that connects the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.Also Read | Amelia Earhart disappeared in 1937. Nearly a century later, why are scientists now investigating a possible clue beneath the water?The fact that there are lots of cables moving along certain paths can be seen as a potential vulnerability. The cables can be damaged by anchors or even subjected to deliberate interference.The data centres are equally vulnerable to such threats. These buildings provide support for the servers that run banking software, governmental services and even artificial intelligence.According to Andreas Krieg, an expert in security studies from King's College London, as reported by Al Jazeera, there is no need for any actual destruction for such buildings to stop functioning.Technology companies have already faced attacksIran’s warning follows earlier statements identifying technology infrastructure as a potential target. Al Jazeera reported that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps named companies including Google, Microsoft, Oracle, Meta and Apple, as well as Emirati AI company G42, in communications outlining potential targets.In March, AWS said two of its facilities in the UAE had been directly struck by drones. A strike near another facility in Bahrain caused physical damage to infrastructure, the company reported.Also Read | In 2019, Amsterdam began using bubble barriers to catch river plastic. Now the US wants to bring the technology to the Great LakesThese incidents demonstrated how attacks can affect commercial services even when their stated objectives are military or political. Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank reported an outage affecting its application during a wider IT disruption, although it did not directly attribute the incident to AWS.Undersea cables have also been damaged during regional conflicts. In February 2024, three cables were cut after the cargo ship Rubymar was disabled by a Houthi missile. Industry assessments linked the damage to the ship’s anchor, while the Houthis denied responsibility for the cable cuts.Two more cables were damaged near Jeddah in September 2025, slowing internet access across parts of the Middle East and South Asia. The cause was not confirmed, according to Al Jazeera.Krieg told the outlet that the attacks exposed the limits of assuming commercial infrastructure would automatically be protected by national air defences.Can the Gulf protect its AI ambitions?The risks matter because technology has become central to Gulf economic diversification plans.The UAE is developing the Stargate UAE AI campus with OpenAI, Nvidia, G42 and other partners.Similar threats confront data centres.Also Read | 2026 Midterm Campaigns: Why some Democratic candidates are keeping Kamala Harris and AOC at a distance while turning to Pete ButtigiegThey provide space for storage of servers that support banking systems, governments, and artificial intelligence systems. Data centres depend on uninterrupted supply of electricity, cooling, and telecommunications.In an interview on Al Jazeera, Andreas Krieg, a security studies expert at King's College London, explained that physical damage is not necessary for the disruption of infrastructure.One response is to develop alternative routes. Iraq signed an agreement with Qatar’s Ooredoo in September to carry data from the Gulf towards Europe through Iraqi territory and Türkiye. Ooredoo’s international arm subsequently agreed to acquire fibre capacity from Iraq’s iQ Networks to extend connectivity, subject to government approval.These would help avoid the use of risky maritime routes, but infrastructure construction is time-consuming.According to Krieg, cited by Al Jazeera, geographical redundancy, even if this involves locations beyond the Gulf, will help build resilience. This poses a problem for governments that would want to maintain control over sensitive data and computing resources within their jurisdiction.Why digital security is becoming a geopolitical issueFor Gulf governments, attracting technology companies is only part of the challenge. They must also convince investors that critical services can continue operating during a regional crisis.In contrast to the AI strategy of the UAE, which depends on American technological firms, the Saudi Arabian and Qatari governments are developing infrastructure that will cater for regional and international clients. Any disruption might impact financial service providers, cloud services and firms far from the zone of conflict.The protection of all cables and data centres may prove to be challenging. Power backups, different network routes and geographical location of the infrastructure can minimise the impacts of any failure. But such efforts demand huge investments.The Houthis’ presence around the Red Sea adds further uncertainty. No direct proof of attacks on internet cables by the group has been found, but engaging in combat in the vicinity of important shipping routes makes the process of fixing damage difficult.The Iranian warning points to how digital infrastructure has come to be both an economic and geopolitical asset.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

Recent escalations have already disrupted Amazon Web Services facilities in the UAE and Bahrain, highlighting the risk. The Gulf has invested significantly in emerging technologies, making security a critical focus for governments and companies. Developing alternative routes for connectivity will be essential to mitigate these threats.

news.title: Kamala Harris Addresses Criticism of Her Laugh: 'You're Not Going to Take My Joy'
news.text:
Former vice president and 2024 Democrat presidential candidate Kamala Harris addressed criticism she has received about her laugh, stating that people are “not going” to take her joy from her.

During an appearance on the Baby, This Is Keke Palmer podcast with host Keke Palmer, Harris was asked how she balances “who Madame VP gets to be as a human and who she has to show up as.” Harris acknowledged that it “can be difficult,” and explained that she “was raised in a family that included very powerful women, who laughed from their bellies.”

“It can be difficult. It can be very difficult, Keke. I’m aware of the, whatever the memes are about my laugh,” Harris said. “Well, look. I was raised in a family that included very powerful women, who laughed from their bellies. And, powerful I mean, they were powerful in their space. They were powerful in their family, in their community. Not necessarily titles and money.”

Harris continued to explain that the women in her family “would sit around the kitchen table with their coffee, laughing loud laughs.”

“Those who try to take your joy are trying to make you weak, and that’s where my fight comes in,” Harris continued. “I know what you’re trying to do, you’re not going to take my joy. There is nothing you can do to me that will take my joy, you are not that powerful.”

While serving as vice president, Harris on several occasions laughed hysterically when delivering speeches, or even when responding to questions from reporters.

Breitbart News reported in August 2021 that Harris “burst into laughter during a speech at a community health center” after she had reminded Americans that “people live in every state”:

She urged more states to expand Medicaid, noting that she and President Joe Biden wanted to expand coverage to cover dental, vision, and hearing as part of his $3.5 trillion entitlement bill disguised as “infrastructure.”
“We also must work together to call on Congress to advance other components of our Build Back agenda. To expand Medicaid in every state … people live in every state.”
“People live in every state. That’s the logic,” she said, before bursting into laughter.

Breitbart News’s Katherine Hamilton reported in August 2021 that when reporters tried to “ask her about Afghanistan” she “busted out in a fit of laughter” and told reporters to “hold on.”
news.summary:
Former vice president and 2024 Democrat presidential candidate Kamala Harris addressed criticism she has received about her laugh, stating that people are "not going" to take her joy from her.

news.title: Ro Khanna Says Billionaires Can ‘Buy’ Democracy. It’s Time to Debunk That Myth.
news.text:
There is a persistent lie in American politics: that any sufficiently rich person can simply buy any election. It sits at the heart of the worldview of our socialist friends on the other side of the aisle and their eternal crusade against the wealthy. They insist that spending money on elections destroys American democracy, that “undue influence” demands yet another stack of special rules, and that wealthy donors single-handedly bend elections to their will. 

That simply isn’t true.

On Monday, California Rep. Ro Khanna blasted SpaceX and Tesla founder Elon Musk for his record spending on Republcians in the 2026 midterm elections, which total to about $366 million, making him the largest known individual donor of the 2026 midterm election cycle. 

"Tax billionaires so they can't buy democracy," Rep. Khanna wrote on X. "Stand with @BernieSanders & me & support a 5% tax on California billionaires. Not with Newsom, Thiel & Musk opposing it."

Tax billionaires so they can't buy democracy. Stand with @BernieSanders & me & support a 5% tax on California billionaires. Not with Newsom, Thiel & Musk opposing it.— Ro Khanna (@RoKhanna) October 12, 2026

The belief that wealth automatically and consistently converts itself into electoral victory suffers from a convenient selection bias, where critics remember the candidate who outspent an opponent and won, and yet forgets the far more common case of candidates or even lobby groups who spent a fortune in an election and still lost. Why is that you may ask? A democratic electorate still has a mind of its own, no matter how much money is spent trying to change it.

Let's take several examples. 

In 2024, Kamala Harris raised and spent more than $1 billion against now-President Donald Trump, yet lost every battleground state and the popular vote. Trump’s campaign spent roughly half as much. 

Just last year, New York City’s wealthy class coalesced against socialist mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani, pouring more than $40 million into stopping him, a historically unprecedented sum. Mamdani won anyway, because he was the candidate voters wanted. 

And just this year in California’s gubernatorial race, progressive billionaire Tom Steyer spent between $213 million and $215 million of his own money, more than six times the next-most-expensive campaign, only to lose to Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton in the primary election.

Now to lobbying in particular. 

In 2021, the pharmaceutical industry spent a record $389 million on federal lobbying, with industry groups on pace to spend roughly $700 million across the 2021-22 cycle as Democrats advanced the Inflation Reduction Act, all to stop Medicare from negotiating prescription-drug prices. That failed. 

In the late 2000s, the ten largest banks in the country spent more than $87 million lobbying Congress from 2009 to 2010 to stop the Dodd-Frank Act. It passed anyway. 

During the same period, health insurers spent $86.2 million opposing the Affordable Care Act, while the broader healthcare sector spent more than $1.1 billion lobbying on the bill in 2009 alone, and yet the ACA passed anyway. 

And tobacco companies spent nearly $73 million on federal lobbying in 1998 alone and roughly $755 million from 1998 through 2020 to oppose smoking regulations and a the Master Settlement Agrrement, and still it did not save them.

Money does not buy elections unless it is combined with popular support, and that support is the necessary ingredient. Without it, all the money in the world cannot change the outcome of an election or a policy fight. 

Yet socialists like Rep. Ro Khanna want you to believe the wealthy possess some irresistible, undue influence over American democracy. They do not. This country was built on representation and on checking concentrated power. Those guardrails do not suddenly vanish the moment someone writes a large campaign check, hires a lobbying firm, or a politician decides it is convenient to pretend otherwise.

news.title: Trump erupts as 'panic' grips White House over stories of his own midterms masterminds cashing in... and Susie Wiles calls crisis meeting
news.text:
Susie Wiles summoned her top advisers to her West Wing office just after 8.15am Friday for a crisis meeting as a wave of stories about Trump allies cashing in on their access threatened to swamp the White House with just weeks before the midterms.

The president's chief of staff was 'panicked,' a source familiar with the meeting told the Daily Mail, as she confronted the political and media fallout from two of the president's top political lieutenants taking lucrative foreign paydays.

Plus, anxiety was building around reports about her own daughters' pro-Russia foreign lobbying work, according to two sources familiar with the mood in the building. 

The White House was blindsided last week by a New York Times report that Chris LaCivita and James Blair, Trump's pair of trusted political hands, had spent the October 4 weekend in the Balkans, advising a Putin-aligned government that had claimed election victory.

It sparked widespread fury as the leaders of Trump's political operation for the 2026 midterms were out of the country scoring handsome consulting fees with just weeks to the election. Republicans are facing strong headwinds to keep their House and Senate majorities and GOP operatives are openly worried.

Wiles first met with her policy right-hand Walker Barrett before assembling other top White House aides, including Megan Bauer, head of Cabinet Affairs, for the early-morning powwow. 

Her message to staff, according to a source: the White House does not engage with the midterms... that's for 'Chris and James' to handle.

Notably, the White House's top media position was still vacant as the negative headlines piled up. Hours later, Trump announced he tapped Katie Zacharia, 41, a pro-MAGA commentator to fill the role of press secretary. 

A White House official pushed back, saying Wiles held her 'usual' morning meetings on Friday, but declined to characterize the nature of the conversations she had with staff. 

But Trump himself is 'furious,' an administration official said, and has been working the phones, calling allies to ask how he should handle the embarrassing disclosure about LaCivita and Blair. 

Days earlier, Trump said he had found no conflict, but behind the scenes that tenor had changed. 

The turmoil has handed Democrats fresh ammunition just as early voting begins and the GOP's grip on Congress looks more flimsy by the October day, Republican operatives confess to the Daily Mail.

The Balkans trip saw LaCivita and Blair travel to Republika Srpska, an entity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, after the Putin-supporting Milorad Dodik claimed victory. It is only one of several headaches Trump is facing. 

The Daily Mail revealed Thursday that Kimberly Guilfoyle, Trump's ambassador to Greece, was under internal investigation over allegations surrounding her potential substance abuse, use of private planes and helicopters, close relationship with an energy and construction company, improper gift acceptance and more. 

Trump himself said he was 'not happy' with the negative press, and on Tuesday, Guilfoyle resigned as ambassador to Greece.

Last week CNN reported on the finances of Jared Kushner, the president's son-in-law, who serves as an unpaid White House adviser, alleging his investments in an Israeli company 'could be a major conflict of interest.' 

The row centered on Affinity Partners, Kushner's private equity firm. Affinity is the largest shareholder of Phoenix Financial, a massive Israeli company worth over $100 billion that handles pensions, insurance and savings for millions.

He fired back in a rare dictum, claiming that he had enough of the media's 'lies.'

Kushner shredded the CNN article for being 'deeply misleading' and noted that Affinity 'does not own the defense companies highlighted in CNN's story.' 

But the damage of the negative press may already have had a big enough impact. 

'The juxtaposition of those stories with the rising cost of gas and everyday goods, it's not a good one,' a senior GOP campaign operative said.

'The timing couldn't be worse. It shows a lack of seriousness from people who are otherwise or purportedly very serious individuals.'

Steve Bannon, a first-term Trump adviser, branded LaCivita and Blair 'grifters' on social media after the story broke.

A representative for LaCivita and Blair was contacted for comment. 

'The average American reports they can't afford to pay their grocery or gas bills,' former Kamala Harris advisor and Democratic strategist Mike Nellis told the Daily Mail. 'Donald Trump is focused on the wrong stuff.'

Democrats on the trail are contrasting voters' squeezed budgets with the fortunes being made in Trump's orbit.

Kushner, who leads US conflict negotiations as a volunteer adviser while overseeing a multi-billion-dollar private equity empire, has been targeted by South Carolina Democratic Senate hopeful Annie Andrews and Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, who dubbed him 'Prince Jared.'

Kushner leads US conflict negotiations as an unpaid adviser while overseeing a multi-billion-dollar private equity firm.

A representative for Kushner was contacted for comment.

Ossoff, who political strategists believe to be laying the groundwork for a 2028 presidential bid, has also gone after the president's close aide Natalie Harp.

'If I'm the Democrats, I'm going to take whatever I can get; it's a midterm election year,' the national GOP operative said. 

Prediction market Kalshi gives Republicans a 38.5 percent chance of holding the Senate and just 10.6 percent of keeping the House. 

Nowhere is the strain clearer than Texas, where the Senate race has already cost $300 million and is on track to reach half a billion, a source familiar with GOP spending told the Daily Mail. 

That is $100 million more than the party's original $400 million estimate.

The bill follows Trump's late endorsement of Attorney General Ken Paxton, who went on to topple incumbent Senator John Cornyn in May's runoff. Cornyn had warned a Paxton nomination would drain resources from other battlegrounds.

'Ken is going to be fine, it's just gonna cost a lot more money than we thought,' the national GOP operative said.

Polls show Paxton neck and neck with Democrat James Talarico. Paxton's campaign was contacted for comment.

The squeeze is being felt in Kansas, which last elected a Democratic senator in 1932. Cook Political Report this week moved Senator Roger Marshall's race against Democrat Adam Hamilton from Lean Republican to Toss Up.

A Democratic-aligned Senate Majority PAC pledged this week to spend $5 million on ads there.

Elsewhere, Alaska and Ohio will be 'knife fights,' Georgia is 'tough' and South Carolina will be fine as long as the GOP 'plays it safe,' the national operative said.

In the House, The Cook Political Report recently re-rated 18 seats in Democrats' favor.

The senior GOP operative blamed two headwinds of the administration's own making: 'Gas prices and the Iran War. Obviously, there are a lot of qualms about that.'

news.summary: Donald Trump's closest allies are cashing in on their proximity to the president as the midterms turn ugly for Republicans, and the bad press is landing on campaigns that were already struggling.

news.title: Dan Le Batard thinks Patrick Mahomes, other athletes are obligated to oppose Trump on Protect College Sports
news.text: Former ESPN host Dan Le Batard is consistent in the standard he applies to when athletes should and should not comment on issues outside of sports. "Speak up for what I agree with or shut up and play ball" is his standard. On Monday, Le Batard shamed Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes for not publicly opposing the Protect College Sports Act, legislation backed by President Donald Trump and his administration. DAN LE BATARD FALSELY CLAIMS THAT ESPN ONLY HIRES AND PAYS WHITE PEOPLE "Patrick Mahomes, get your helmet out of your a--. Do some leading here," an emotional Le Batard shouted on YouTube. "You’ve got a lot of power ... do you want to participate in the adult games, or do you just want to play football?" To answer that question, Mahomes just wants to play football. He has said so. Following the 2024 shooting at the Chiefs' Super Bowl parade, Mahomes led not with activism but with actions. He donated money to an aid fund for victims and visited some of the wounded in the hospital. He later explained in a Time Magazine profile that he does not believe it is his place to shift public opinion on complicated political issues like gun control. "I continue to educate myself," Mahomes said of the issue. "I don't want to make a quick response to something that takes a lot of education to really learn and make a swaying comment based off that. But I know we have to find a solution of some way to make this stuff stop." Likewise, Mahomes declined to endorse a candidate in the 2024 presidential election. "I don’t want to pressure anyone to vote for a certain president," he told the outlet. "I want people to use their voice, whoever they believe in. I want them to do the research." Perhaps his restraint is partly why the Chiefs surpassed the Dallas Cowboys as the leading national draw in the NFL. Like Michael Jordan, Mahomes is polarizing because of his greatness, not because he has deliberately divided his audience along political lines. Jordan and Mahomes are arguably the two biggest individual draws in the recent history of their respective sports. That is not a coincidence. More importantly, Patrick Mahomes does not owe anyone an opinion on legislation. He doesn't owe anyone an opinion on anything but his own actions. The amusing part is that if Mahomes spoke out in support of the bill, Le Batard would almost certainly demand his silence. He'd then call on the media to hold Mahomes accountable. That's how Le Batard responded when Jaxson Dart introduced President Trump on stage, Aaron Rodgers questioned the effectiveness of the COVID vaccines and various UFC fighters embraced Trump. Do you notice a pattern? Le Batard presents his personal political preferences as universal moral imperatives. He sees silence as cowardice when he wants an athlete to speak. news.title: Democrats Are Terrified of Kamala Harris
news.text:
Harris has offered voters almost nothing in the way of specifics about how she would remake a Democratic Party hungry for change after another term of Donald Trump. She hasn’t spoken to how she would expand her own appeal to the voters who rejected her and she remains as reticent of media as ever, continuing to favor appearances before friendly audiences and at times drawing fire for shutting out news organizations altogether. She has entirely sidestepped the ideological civil war consuming the Democrats and has acted more like a party elder at a time when voters and donors are demanding a break with the past.

“I don’t see anything different myself. It seems like more of the same to me,” said Jim Hodges, the former governor of South Carolina, the first state on the Democratic nominating calendar. “Right now Democratic primary voters … are very anxious about a Trump acolyte being in the White House in 2028. And they want to select someone who they think has the best chance to win, but who also meets these requisites: fresh, new. I hear a lot of talk about that — ‘we don’t need recycled candidates.’”

Many of Harris’ supporters are coming to that same conclusion, including in her home state, where several donors told POLITICO they’re actively shopping for candidates to back and have no desire to see Harris run. Even some who say they’d ultimately support Harris if she prevails are doubtful she can break through.

“I am looking at all kinds of candidates for 2028, and she’s not necessarily one of them,” said Laurie Black, a San Diego-based donor and longtime Harris supporter. “It’s not that I don’t think she’s qualified … [but] I want to support a winner in 2028, and I just don’t know if the vice president has the juice this time.”

Another California-based fundraiser could not think of a single person in their circle who wants Harris to run again.

“She probably could raise grassroots money because she has fabulous lists,” said the fundraiser, who was granted anonymity to discuss private conversations. “But there are no obvious big donors that have indicated they want to go down that route.”

Saudi Arabia is one of the largest spenders on military matters in the world, relying on highly advanced weaponry from America and Europe for the defence of its cities, oil facilities, and military establishments. However, several attacks using missiles and drones conducted by Houthi rebels from Yemen revealed the complexity of the problem of protecting the country from its determined enemy. The recent attack on the airports of Riyadh and Abha has brought this point into question.As reported by CNN in October, the Houthis have shown their capability to target vital facilities despite other attacks being intercepted by the Saudi troops. This is in addition to the disruption caused at the airports as well as fears regarding the safety of vital facilities.Also Read | Amelia Earhart disappeared in 1937. Nearly a century later, why are scientists now investigating a possible clue beneath the water?As much as $83 billion was allocated for defence by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 2025, based on information provided by CNN and the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. Some of the defence systems in use include Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defence (THAAD) systems, as well as other sophisticated warplanes.The challenge is not simply the quality of those weapons. Saudi Arabia must protect an enormous area, with threats approaching from several directions and a growing number of potential targets.Live EventsThe recent attacks illustrate why military spending alone cannot guarantee that every incoming missile or drone will be stopped.Why Saudi Arabia's advanced air defences face a difficult testSaudi Arabia's security problem extends well beyond its capital. Airports, oil refineries, pipelines, military bases and other essential facilities are spread across a vast territory. Each requires protection against weapons that can approach at different altitudes, speeds and directions.There are dangers posed to the state from Yemen on the southern side of the state, dangers posed to the state by Iran through the Gulf on the eastern side and dangers posed to the state by Iran-backed militias from Iraq on the northern side of the state.According to CNN, there have been missile strikes through the use of ballistic missiles and cruise missiles, and even drone strikes, posing challenges to the ability of the state to detect and counter any such threats.Also Read | In 2019, Amsterdam began using bubble barriers to catch river plastic. Now the US wants to bring the technology to the Great LakesThere are various kinds of missiles which pose various challenges. Ballistic missiles are very fast, while cruise missiles are capable of travelling low and slow. Drones can be used in combination with missile strikes.Interceptor technology is limited, although quite sophisticated. The defending force must be able to identify the weapon, track its path and intercept it before it hits its target. With multiple weapons coming at you, it gets all the more difficult.Saudi Arabia has managed to intercept many weapons; however, the recent attacks on the airport reveal that mere interception counts do not tell the whole story.How the Houthis have developed their missile and drone capabilitiesFor many years, the Houthis have been building their capabilities to become able to threaten distant targets, which lie outside the territory they control in Yemen. These include ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones with range-flying capabilities.UN experts have confirmed that missile parts and other military equipment that originate from Iran are provided to the Houthis despite the arms embargo imposed on them by the international community. Some similarities exist between the arms used by the Houthis and Iranian-made missiles.Also Read | 2026 Midterm Campaigns: Why some Democratic candidates are keeping Kamala Harris and AOC at a distance while turning to Pete ButtigiegCNN's reporting has highlighted the group's use of combined attacks to put pressure on air defences. A barrage involving drones and different types of missiles can complicate the task of identifying, tracking and intercepting each incoming weapon.The Houthis have also drawn lessons from years of fighting Saudi Arabia and other opponents.In fact, their tactic will not require them to equip themselves on par with the country’s military arsenal on a one-to-one basis. Rather, they can employ cheaper drones and missiles against vital infrastructure facilities, causing transport disruption and forcing Saudi Arabia to invest in its defence.These actions will have implications that go beyond military bases. The destruction of any airport may cause disruption and affect people’s morale, while strikes against oil infrastructure will impact energy operations and market psychology.In fact, the connection between Iran and the Houthis makes the conflict even more complex. At the same time, Houthis have their own political aspirations, connected with Yemen’s prolonged civil war and conflict with Saudi Arabia, and not everything can be explained just by following Tehran’s orders.Saudi Arabia faces a choice between escalation and diplomacyThese attacks will put Riyadh in a tight corner. Although it may show Saudi Arabia’s seriousness toward attacks on its territory, it might result in more attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities, and other vital centres of the country.Saudi Arabia has been making efforts to ease regional tension for quite some time now and gain investments from around the world. The economic blueprint of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman depends in part on Saudi Arabia being seen as a haven for tourism, the tech industry, etc.Also Read | Elon Musk's $366 million political spending surge: Why he's backing Republicans in 2026 midtermsRepeated security incidents threaten that ambition. The danger is not confined to the oil industry: airports, data centres, desalination plants and transport networks are all important to the country's economic development.CNN's October coverage has described the growing pressure on Saudi Arabia as the conflict with the Houthis intensifies. The kingdom must weigh the benefits of military action against the risk of a wider confrontation and the possibility that further strikes could follow.Riyadh is also seeking greater international support. Regional partners may provide defensive assistance, while Saudi Arabia could pursue additional weapons and interceptors from Western suppliers.But replenishing stocks is not straightforward. The United States has also faced pressure on its own munitions inventories following recent military operations, according to reporting cited in the supplied CNN article.A ground offensive against the Houthis would present further difficulties. The group is entrenched in Yemen, has extensive combat experience and operates in challenging mountainous terrain.Experience has proven that mere air power will not be enough to eliminate it as an influence on the battlefield.This means that diplomacy is still an available method for achieving peace, even if it turns out to be a tough process. In order to find an agreement, it will be necessary to take into account the claims of the Houthis, the security needs of Saudi Arabia, and the overall situation in Yemen.The huge budget of Saudi Arabia, which equals $83 billion, has ensured its access to highly advanced weaponry, yet no matter how complex an air-defence system is, it cannot provide full protection of such a large area. news.title: Texas' Biggest Country Artists Back James Talarico Over Ken Paxton
news.text: Kacey Musgraves is the latest major country music star from Texas to throw her support behind Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico. Musgraves hosted Talarico at her concert in Dallas at the weekend, later rallying behind him in a social media spat with former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem. Her endorsement follows others for Talarico from some of the most recognizable names in Texas music. Country music legend Willie Nelson, who has long supported Democratic candidates and progressive causes, endorsed Talarico in a video released by the Talarico campaign last week. “Hi, this is Wille Nelson,” the 93-year-old singer said in the video. “I’ve gotten to know James Talarico. He’s a good man who will be a good senator for the state of Texas. Please vote and vote for James Talarico.” Earlier this month The Chicks, who were formed in Dallas, endorsed Talarico by sharing a photo on Instagram wearing "I'm a Talafreako" shirts. "Get Ur Freak On," they wrote in the caption, tagging Talarico and providing key dates for Texas voters to know. Taken together, the endorsements provide Talarico with a significant advantage given the unique role that country music plays in Texas' culture, with some of the state’s biggest stars publicly on his side as he seeks to become the first Democrat elected to the Senate in Texas since 1988. Notably, no country music star of similar prominence has publicly endorsed his Republican opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Newsweek has contacted the Talarico and Paxton campaigns for comment. Country Music Cuts Across Social Lines Nadine Hubbs, a cultural historian and professor at the University of Michigan, told Newsweek that country music is popular in Texas in a way that is different from virtually anywhere else in the country, and its popularity cuts across social and economic divides. ”Rich people like country music, poor people like country music, people in the middle like country music," Hubbs said. “It’s a really big state and they have a really distinct culture and country music is part of it.” Because of that, Hubbs believes endorsements from artists such as Nelson and Musgraves bode well for Talarico. She noted it is especially significant given the attacks Talarico faced from Paxton and Republicans over his absence from the campaign trail while recovering from the flu. “If you're in Texas, country music is a loud force in Texas and it does make a difference if you're kind of casually paying attention and you see all the pictures that are circulating today with James Talarico with his arm respectfully around the beautiful Kasey Musgraves, Hubbs said. 'Nobody Wants to Touch Ken Paxton' “He's back out in circulation and immediately he's on stage at a huge concert Saturday with Kasey Musgraves... The casual kind of voter will see this and, just kind of feel it, even if they don't want to read about it, that one guy is touchable, the other guy's untouchable. Kacey Musgraves is touching James Talarico. Nobody wants to touch Ken Paxton, either literally or figuratively.” But some Republicans have sought to diminish the endorsements. Texas Senator Ted Cruz responded to Nelson's endorsement by suggesting it would doom Talarico's camapaign. "Willie’s music is great, but historically, this has been the beginning of the end for Democrat campaigns in Texas….," he wrote on X. And Noem, the former Homeland Security Secretary, decided to wade into Texas politics after Musgraves hosted Talarico at her concert by saying she prefers Ella Langley to Musgraves. "I’ll take @ellalangleymsic over Kacey Musgraves any day. And if I’m choosin’ Texas, I’ll take Ken Paxton over James Talarico," Noem wrote. Musgraves hit back with an apparent reference to a controversial anecdote Noem included in her memoir about killing her 14-month-old dog, Cricket. "I don't think you have a dog in this fight but if you did you would have shot it," Musgraves wrote on X Can Celebrity Endorsements Matter? Celebrity endorsements rarely transform races on their own, but experts say they can help shape voter perceptions and engage audiences that candidates might otherwise struggle to reach. David Jackson, a professor of American government at Bowling Green State University whose research focuses on the links between culture and politics, told Newsweek that successful celebrity endorsements generally depend on three factors: name recognition, public affection and credibility. "The celebrity has to be well known within the target audience," Jackson said. “Second, people have to like the celebrity. Finally, there is credibility. Target audiences must find the celebrity endorser credible on politics and policy.” Jackson said endorsements from celebrities are like other cues that voters use to make decisions, similar to those offered by party leaders, media outlets or interest groups. Costas Panagopoulos, a political science professor at Northeastern University, said celebrity endorsements can be especially impactful because they reach people who may not be closely following politics. "The effect would likely be modest, but even this can be decisive in tight races,” he told Newsweek. James Talarico Vs. Ken Paxton: Latest Polls Talarico has led most polls since Paxton clinched the nomination, usually inside the margin of error. The RealClearPolitics average of polls has him leading by 3 points—48.1 percent to Paxton's 45.1 percent—as of Tuesday. The ReconMR Texas Poll, the newest poll in that average, found Talarico with a four-point lead over Paxton, 48 percent to 44 percent. The survey was conducted October 5 to 8 among 617 likely voters and has a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. A poll from the Republican-leaning Trafalgar Group, conducted among 1,086 likely voters from October 6 to 8, largely during Talarico's absence from the campaign trail, found Talarico ahead of Paxton, 47 percent to 44 percent. A YouGov and a New York Times/Siena College poll each had him ahead by six points in early October, and a late-September Fox News poll put him two points ahead of Paxton. Paxton has polled better on the border. A Texas Pulse poll by the Texas A&M Bush School and ReconMR in late July found him ahead 48 percent to 44 percent on securing the U.S.-Mexico border. Democrats are treating Talarico's lead with caution. In interviews with Newsweek published Sunday, party strategists warned that narrow edges in Texas and other Senate races could vanish, pointing to 2024, when Kamala Harris' September lead was gone by November. "Every Democrat should be running as if they're 10 points behind," Doug Gordon, a Democratic strategist and co-founder of UpShift Strategies, told Newsweek. Contact Newsweek editor on this story: Edward Pearcey.
news.summary: Kacey Musgraves and Willie Nelson are among the country stars who have endorsed James Talarico in the Senate race.

news.title: ‘SNL’ Star Michael Che Uses MAGA’s Favorite Slur to Mortify Donald Trump
news.text:
Saturday Night Live star Michael Che is flipping the script on MAGA’s obsession with the “r-slur.” 

In his new Netflix stand-up special, Michael Che: Shot in Minnesota, the “Weekend Update” anchor explained why the word has enjoyed renewed popularity among the MAGA base—and how President Trump’s critics could be using it to their advantage.

Trump has repeatedly referred to his predecessor Joe Biden as “mentally r----ded,” and even reportedly called his opponent Kamala Harris the slur back in the 2024 election. 

White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, meanwhile, called the Daily Beast’s Chief Content Officer Joanna Coles “a r----d who has no idea what goes on in the White House” in response to her comments about the Trump administration on The Daily Beast Podcast.

Che jokingly made the argument that liberals, by declining to use the offensive term, have unwittingly let the MAGA movement off the hook. 

“Ever since we stopped using the word r----ded, r----ded people have taken over the world,” Che joked. “I don’t think that s--t’s a coincidence. I think if we still used the word r----ded, Donald Trump could have never been president.”

Che explained his theory further: “That’s why he won. We didn’t have a word to call him.”

Che recalled the many presidential debates where Trump’s opponents struggled to explain exactly why Trump wasn’t a good fit for office. 

“‘Come on, this guy can’t be president. He’s clearly...’ Like, just say it,” Che said. Instead of using terms like “unpresidential,” Che argued, Trump’s opponents should’ve just said, “He’s a r----ded guy.”

“R----ded meaning regressive,” Che clarified. “A bunch of motherf---ers trying to take all our rights away.”

Che then set his sights not just on Trump but the entire MAGA movement: “Trump’s not just dangerous because he’s r----ded, he’s also... He’s like a r----d whisperer.”

Referencing the Jan. 6 riots where Trump supporters stormed the Capitol in an attempt to overthrow the results of the 2020 election, Che said that Trump “knows exactly what to say to get r----ed people to just dress up like Vikings and start storming s--t.” 

“Why do you think they spend so much money on hats?” he asked. “R----ed guys love hats. And Donald Trump makes the greatest r----ded hat: Fire engine red. You give a r----ded guy a free hat, you have made a friend for life.”

Che’s special, which also covered controversial topics like the Charlie Kirk assassination, was notably more explicit than his usual material behind SNL’s “Weekend Update” desk. 

After doing a particularly risqué assassination joke about a gay John Wilkes Booth, Che confessed, “This is why they don’t let me do sketches on Saturday Night Live.”

Getty ImagesIn 1937, Amelia Earhart vanished while flying around the world. 89 years later, her disappearance remains unresolved despite searches, theories and new expeditions

Almost 90 years after the disappearance of aviation pioneer Amelia Earhart on a mission to circumnavigate the globe, experts have arrived at a distant island in the Pacific to inspect an oddity which may provide fresh clues regarding her last flight. The expedition team, consisting of 17 members from the Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) and Purdue University, has reached the Republic of Kiribati’s Nikumaroro Island on October 12 following a five-day journey of about 830 nautical miles.Their target is a formation known as the Taraia Object, first noticed in satellite imagery in 2020.Also Read | In 2019, Amsterdam began using bubble barriers to catch river plastic. Now the US wants to bring the technology to the Great LakesAs the BBC reported, some researchers believe the object could be the remains of Earhart’s Lockheed Electra aircraft. Others question that interpretation, arguing that the shape may be a fallen tree rather than an aeroplane.The expedition is expected to spend five days examining the site, using archaeological equipment to investigate what lies beneath the lagoon’s sediment. The findings could strengthen one of several theories about Earhart’s disappearance, although the team has yet to establish what the object actually is.Live EventsThe Taraia Object puts a new lead under investigationThe investigation centres on a feature near the edge of a lagoon on Nikumaroro’s Taraia Peninsula. The strange formation was recognised through satellite pictures taken in 2020 as well as pictures taken at an earlier time which seem to show the same formation.As the BBC has reported, the object is situated near the coastline, possibly around ten feet from the shore and submerged by just five feet of water, based on the tides.Also Read | 2026 Midterm Campaigns: Why some Democratic candidates are keeping Kamala Harris and AOC at a distance while turning to Pete ButtigiegSediment may cover part or all of the formation.Expedition leader Rick Pettigrew has spent years examining the possibility that the object is connected to Earhart’s aircraft.Purdue University has been cooperating with the investigation process thanks to its historical connection to the aviator, who once worked there and received financial backing from Purdue for her Lockheed Electra.The group intends to search the area around the submerged object for artefacts before investigating it. While the object’s appearance in historical pictures justifies further investigation, it doesn’t necessarily mean that it belongs to an aircraft.How researchers plan to examine the possible wreckageThe expedition is using several methods to determine the object’s composition and position beneath the water.Researchers will first survey the area systematically, recording potential artefacts and marking out search lines. A magnetometer will then be used to detect ferrous metals, including steel components that might be associated with an aircraft. Although the Lockheed Electra was largely made of aluminium, other parts could produce detectable readings.Also Read | Elon Musk's $366 million political spending surge: Why he's backing Republicans in 2026 midtermsThe team also plans to use sonar equipment to locate objects beneath the lagoon floor. A probe will help investigators assess the target’s depth, orientation and surface characteristics. Sediment may then be removed with specialised dredging equipment to allow a direct visual inspection.As the BBC has reported, the work will depend heavily on weather, sea conditions and tides. The researchers must also transport equipment across difficult terrain, including a jungle trail that the crew plans to clear.The immediate objective is to determine what the Taraia Object is. Any attempt to recover aircraft components would require additional permission from the Kiribati government.Giant coconut crabs and difficult conditions complicate the searchReaching Nikumaroro was itself a major undertaking. The team travelled aboard the Marin Mainiku, a vessel that carried researchers across the South Pacific to the uninhabited atoll.The expedition must now contend with changing ocean conditions and the effects of El Niño, which could restrict safe access to the shore. Marine archaeologist Michael Krivor has expressed concern about weather patterns that could make travel through narrow reef channels dangerous.Wildlife presents another unusual challenge.The coconut crabs, or the robber crabs, live on Nikumaroro and come out at night searching for food. The coconut crabs are among the largest of the land crustaceans and have the ability to climb trees and break coconuts, among other animals.BBC reports indicate that the scientists will be sleeping on the ship rather than on the island overnight.This will not only help them in dealing with safety issues but also address the logistical problems in an isolated area.The researchers have very limited time available for their project; therefore, the weather forecast, tides, and boat transportation are crucial for them.What the search could reveal about Earhart’s disappearanceIt was July 2, 1937, when Amelia Earhart disappeared while trying to be the first lady to circle the Earth. Both Amelia Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan had managed to cover many countries before setting off from Lae, Papua New Guinea, to land on Howland Island.As can be seen, it is evident that there was some problem with radio contact in finding the destination. It appears that the theory about the case is that the fuel in the aircraft ran out and it must have crashed somewhere in the Pacific Ocean; however, there is no concrete evidence for the same as of now.There is another theory that Earhart and Noonan landed at Nikumaroro, where they may have lived like castaways.However, the Taraia Object has its own sceptics. Ric Gillespie, a veteran investigator of the Earhart mystery, believes the formation is a fallen pandanus tree. That interpretation has not been resolved by the new expedition.As the BBC’s reporting makes clear, the search remains an investigation rather than a confirmed discovery. Identifying the object could help researchers assess one possible explanation for Earhart’s fate, but a definitive conclusion will depend on physical evidence and careful analysis.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!
