news.title: School board race rocked over sexist AI ad showing female candidate surrounded by cakes at bake sale
news.text:
A California school board race has sparked controversy after a trustee candidate allegedly used a sexist artificial intelligence advertisement against his opponent.

David Ray Miyashiro is going up against Amy Flicker on November 3 for a trustee seat on the San Dieguito Union High School District.

Flicker is a former Encinitas Planning and Environmental commissioner, and Miyashiro is the superintendent of the Cajon Valley School District.

But the President of the San Dieguito Faculty Association, a labor union, has now claimed that Miyashiro used artificial intelligence 'to generate deceptive, sexist imagery to attack candidate Amy Flicker' in his campaign flyer on October 11. 

The promotional flyer included in the news release allegedly showed a side-by-side photo of the candidates. 

On the left side, Flicker was standing in front of a table with baked goods with the words 'Non-Profit volunteer,' written below her. On the right-side Miyashiro sat in front of a microphone with the words 'District superintendent,' printed below him. 

It stated: 'The choice is obvious. Who is more qualified to be a school board trustee in Sand Dieguito?'

'Using AI technology to manipulate the likeness of a female candidate and diminish my public service into a condescending stereotype is both ethically dubious and deeply concerning for someone seeking a position in educational leadership,' Flicker wrote in the SDFA news release. 

All current members in SDUHD office are not seeking re-election. The school members who will depart include the current President Jane Lea Smith, Trustee Phan Anderson and Vice President Rimga Viskanta. 

Viskanta has been in the running for Mayor of Encinitas, while Flicker has been endorsed by the SDFA. The SDFA represents over 600 educators and staff in the district. 

'Rimga Viskanta, who currently holds the seat, asked me to run for her seat,' Flicker said. 

'I have always wanted to be in this position. I've always wanted to be a trustee, so this isn't some fly by night thing that I decided to do. This is … a long time coming,' Flicker told the Torrey Pines High School Falconer.

'Rimga Viskanta, who currently holds the seat, asked me to run for her seat,' Flicker said.

According to the Falconer, Flicker has prioritized being 'very literary with AI and where it's evolving to,' during her campaign.

'Students using AI to help them with homework has jumped to in one year. Students globally are using it at a rate of 69 percent in one year. What I'm concerned about is how AI is being integrated, and if we are staying as much ahead of the curve as possible,' Flicker told the paper. 

'Anybody that tells [you] that they're ahead of the AI curve is either a fool or they're lying because it is racing at such a pace that it's hard to remain literate in it. I do believe that we need a board that is literate as much as humanly possible in AI to bring that into the classroom, bring it into student's lives and do it responsibly,' Flicker said. 

Miyashiro has not publicly made comments in his campaign on his stance on AI usage but has emphasized listening to students' voices and needs. 

'Policy should be driven by the people. In this day and age, lots of people come in with their own agendas … I think that's the wrong standpoint. The standpoint could be: ‘I'm going to really meet the students, I'm going to really listen to staff and to see what they need to be successful for our students,' Miysashiro told the paper. 

The Daily Mail has reached out to David Ray Miyashiro, Amy Flicker and Rimga Viskanta for comments.

During this year, the use of AI for campaigning material has been a polarizing issue that has affected other Californian elections such as the governor race in the 2026 midterms. 

Republican candidate Steve Hilton has utilized AI-generated videos of his opponent, Xavier Becerra, Governor Gavin Newsom and Kamala Harris in his advertisements. 

According to the Fair Political Practices Commission, Californian candidates must clearly disclose if their campaign ads use AI or are substantially altered. 

'If a committee creates, originally publishes, or originally distributes an ad that contains any image that is generated or substantially altered using artificial intelligence, a disclosure stating: “Ad generated or substantially altered using artificial intelligence.” is required,' the Fair Political Practices Commission stated. 

Over $16 million has been spent on television ads that use AI-generated or manipulated content in the 2026 midterm campaigns, according to CNN. 

'Our school district should be modeling digital citizenship, integrity, and media literacy for our students—not using generative AI tools to mislead voters and target female leaders,' Flicker wrote in the SDFA news release.

The Daily Mail has reached out to the San Dieguito Faculty Association and the San Dieguito Union High School District for comments.
news.summary: David Ray Miyashiro is going up against Amy Flicker on November 3 for a trustee seat on the San Dieguito Union High School District.

news.title: Elon Musk Pumps $366M Into Midterms as World's Richest Man Goes All-in on Republican Congress
news.text: Elon Musk has spent about £274 million ($366 million) in the 2026 US midterm election cycle, making him likely the largest known political donor in this year's races.More than £207 million ($276 million) of that went to Republican groups and his own super PAC between July and September alone, according to campaign finance records reported by The New York Times and Reuters.The total already exceeds the roughly £217 million ($290 million) Musk spent in 2024 and reverses his pledge last year to spend 'a lot less' on politics.Where the Money WentThe largest single cheque, £118 million ($158 million), went to the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, Reuters reported.Musk also put £57 million ($76 million) into his own America PAC and £15 million ($20 million) into the Congressional Leadership Fund, which is aligned with House Speaker Mike Johnson.Smaller sums went to Lone Star Liberty PAC, which supports Ken Paxton's Senate campaign in Texas, where recent polls show a close race with Democrat James Talarico, and the Republican Governors Association, each receiving £7.5 million ($10 million).The Republican Attorneys General Association received £1.5 million ($2 million). An America PAC spokesman confirmed the breakdown.The remaining £67 million ($90 million) or so of Musk's reported cycle spending went toward work tied to the previous election or other political causes, Reuters said, citing an America PAC spokesman.Those activities included Brad Schimel, the conservative candidate who lost Wisconsin's Supreme Court election in April 2025, and a £750,000 ($1 million) programme that paid registered voters who signed a petition backing free speech and gun rights.Musk also gave through groups that do not disclose their donors, the Times reported, so the full total may be higher. The cycle began on 1 January 2025. Many super PACs must disclose third-quarter spending on Thursday, which will make the new giving public.Musk's contribution to the Senate Leadership Fund alone exceeded the £113 million ($151 million) that Senate Majority PAC, its main Democratic rival, raised in the third quarter.Senate Majority PAC entered October with roughly £84 million to £94 million ($112 million to $126 million) in cash, the Daily Caller reported. America PAC is backing Republican candidates in seven battleground states and nearly three dozen House races.From 'Done Enough' to All-InThe spending reverses the course Musk set out in 2025. Speaking at the Qatar Economic Forum in May that year, shortly before leaving his role in the Trump administration, he said he planned to spend 'a lot less' on future elections, Time reported. 'If I see a reason to do political spending in the future, I will do it. I do not currently see a reason,' he said.Weeks later, Musk and Donald Trump fell out publicly over Trump's flagship tax and spending bill, which Musk called a 'disgusting abomination'. Musk then threatened to set up a third political party.He vowed to help defeat lawmakers who voted for Trump's spending bill 'if it is the last thing I do on this Earth' and signalled support for Republican Representative Thomas Massie, who Time reported later lost his primary.Time reported that the new donations signal an effort to improve his relationship with Trump and the party.America PAC spokesman Andrew Romeo said the group's 'robust investments have allowed the G.O.P. apparatus to get its message out'.Musk ranked first on Forbes' 2026 World's Billionaires list, which estimated his net worth at about £628 billion ($839 billion), The Standard reported.In the 2024 cycle, when Trump defeated Kamala Harris, Musk spent roughly £217 million ($290 million).Much of that earlier money also flowed through America PAC, which in the final weeks of the 2024 race offered £750,000 ($1 million) a day to registered voters in swing states who signed its petition.Philadelphia's district attorney challenged the giveaway in court. Musk went on to lead the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) from January 2025 until he left the administration at the end of May that year.Democrats Eye SubpoenasThe money comes as Democrats' chances of retaking the House and Senate improve, according to Reuters. Control of either chamber would give them subpoena power, although proposed investigations are not findings of wrongdoing.House Democrats have called for investigations into government contracts held by Musk's companies, worth tens of billions of dollars, and into his work running DOGE. Republicans have blocked several Democratic attempts to subpoena him, Time reported.New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman said Democrats had privately told her they planned to subpoena Musk over DOGE if they won the power to do so, Time reported.Musk rejects claims that his companies depend on federal contracts. Disputing them, he wrote on X on 2 October that 'roughly 90% of SpaceX's revenue this year will be commercial' and that 'SpaceX is FAR MORE commercial relative to the average company in America'. Voters go to the polls on 3 November, with every House seat and about a third of the Senate on the ballot.

news.title: Final Pike County suspect will face trial in Seneca County
news.text:
This story has been updated with additional details about the ruling.

George "Billy" Wagner III, the alleged mastermind of the 2016 massacre in Pike County, will be tried in Seneca County in the northwest part of the state, according to a new ruling in the case.

Wagner, due for trial in January, sought and won a change of venue in November 2024.

In an Oct. 13 court entry, Visiting Judge Jonathan Hein said he selected Seneca County, in part, for demographics, heritage and remoteness similar to Pike County.

Seneca is located about an hour south of Toledo and about three hours from Pike County.

Wagner attorney Mark Collins said he was thankful for the ruling.

"Changing venue is the only way to protect our client’s right to a fair trial," he said via email. "We look forward to start of the trial on Jan. 11." 

Special Prosecutor Angela Canepa did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the decision.

In an earlier filing, Canepa said the judge floated the idea of Seneca County in August 2024 during a meeting with lawyers in his chambers.

Wagner is facing eight counts of aggravated murder and 14 related charges in the 2016 shooting deaths of seven members of the Rhoden family and one future member. He has been jailed since his arrest in November 2018, held in Butler County until September 2024 and Pickaway County since then.

Seneca jury pool less 'tainted' by publicity, judge says

In addition to its demographics, Hein, in his ruling, said he selected Seneca County because:

Potential jurors should be less impacted by "the taint from prior publicity" in the case.Facilities include secure, ADA-compliant courtrooms with experienced court personnel.Hotels and restaurants can accommodate lawyers, witnesses, victim family members and media.

The Seneca County Common Pleas Court, located at 103 E. Market St., has two elected judges and two magistrates. The general division hears felony and some civil cases; the domestic division handles divorce, custody and child support cases.

The traditional, three-story red brick courthouse opened in 2018. It sits in the middle downtown, two blocks east of the Sandusky River, which cuts a north-south path through the center of the city.

Tiffin (nickname “T-town”) is the county seat, home to about 18,000 of the county’s 54,000 residents.

Of the 25,000 Seneca County residents who voted in the November 2024 presidential election, 68% picked Donald Trump and 31% Kamala Harris.

news.title: Bill Maher Confirms Upcoming Second Dinner With Trump: 'He Was, Like, Really Nice'
news.text:
“Real Time” host Bill Maher announced on Monday’s episode of his “Club Random” podcast that he will once again break bread with President Donald Trump, who publicly trashed the comedian following their first private White House meal together last year.

“I’m having dinner with him again next week, by the way,” Maher said.

Maher came under scrutiny for dining with Trump in March 2025, as the president had already taken steps toward dismantling the Department of Education and had launched mass deportations and federal immigration raids across the U.S.

The HBO host later stated Trump was “gracious and measured” during their dinner, but assured viewers that he would continue fairly criticizing the president on his show. Trump went on to slam Maher on social media, but has now purportedly invited him back.

Maher said during his podcast that Trump did so over the phone “out of the blue.”

“I was like, great!” Maher said. “And he was, like, really nice. Like, ‘I promise I won’t say bad things about you like I did the last time.’ And I texted back and I said, ‘You know what? You’re the president of the United States, say whatever the fuck you want.’”

He continued, “I’m just glad we’re talking. … It’s just what he does. It’s how he talks.”

Maher made the comments during a conversation with billionaire Hollywood power broker Ari Emanuel, who noted he himself has met with Trump “to get things done.” Maher, who was called out by comedian Larry David following his first Trump dinner, agreed with that stance.

“It blows my mind that there are people in this world, and lots of them on the far left, who just would turn this opportunity down,” Maher told Emanuel. “A private dinner in the White House with the president, just a few people. Say whatever you want.”

He added, “I’ve heard people say, ‘Well, I don’t like the war.’ Tell him! You can tell him, and I will.”

Maher argued “there’s a way to talk to Donald Trump” and pushed back against criticism that he is humanizing the president. The self-described atheist said Trump is “very flawed,” adding that “we all are, under Jesus.”

The “Real Time” host notably supported the Iran war following initial joint U.S.-Israeli strikes in February and slammed former Vice President Kamala Harris for speaking out against it, only to urge Trump to “cut and run” when the president’s promises of a swift victory crumbled.

news.title: AI predicts which of the potential 2028 presidential candidate is most likely to win the White House
news.text:
The next president is soon to make an appearance when the elections happen in two years, so it’s a good thing technology has an idea of who is likely to rule the country to give you time to prepare. 

The 2028 presidential candidate pool is growing, and while it isn’t official who will be running, you know the frontrunners already. 

For example, when it comes to the Democratic and Republican primaries, a Focaldata and Financial Times poll has all the answers about who is set to go head-to-head. 

Released on Sunday (October 11), it shows some familiar figures from the past and present could be about to try their luck at winning the election. 

Former Vice President Kamala Harris and current Vice President JD Vance are both at the top of their respective party’s idea of who could run for POTUS, per the poll. 

According to the survey, Harris has a 30 per cent support, while Vance has a 38 per cent support from the Republicans. 

From there, there is California Governor Gavin Newsom being favored by 15 per cent of Democrats, and then and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg having nine per cent of backing. 

As for Republicans, behind Vance is Secretary of State Marco Rubio (24%), and with Florida Governor Ron DeSantis finishing last (9%). 

Betting companies also have similar views on who could end up winning the election based on who is leading with voters. 

Polymarket published the following predictions on its site for betters to take note of: 

20% to Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez 13% to Jon Ossoff 10% to Gavin Newsom 8% to Marco Rubio 

But when it comes to the winner of the 2028 election, AI doesn’t think any of the Democrats are likely to fare well. 

In fact, it places its trust in Vance being named the next POTUS and here’s why. 

Calling him ‘the single likeliest candidate in these markets,’ AI revealed that this is because of several factors, including his relationship with the current sitting president – Donald Trump – and with a base of ‘voters who favour stricter immigration policies, economic nationalism, and an “America First” approach’, Vance could ‘inherit much of that support.’ 

However, the tide could very well change for Vance if things like 'inflation, housing costs, or unemployment remain major concerns.’ 

Then, it says Vance could be blamed for the economic struggle just by being associated with Trump and the Republican party. 

Right now, per a Reuters/ Ipsos poll which asked Americans whether or not they approve of Trump, only 35 per cent said yes. 

With Trump’s September approval rating standing with a 35 per cent approval and 59 per cent disapproval, it’s not looking great for the party. 

Per figures released from YouGov's 'Direction of the United States' tracker, 64.4 per cent of respondents said the country is 'off track,' while 29.8 per cent said it is moving in the right direction. 

So, it depends on how well Trump does.

news.title: House Republicans appear to have an open-seat problem
news.text:
ANALYSIS -- With President Donald Trump’s national job approval rating hovering near 37 percent, it’s no surprise that dozens of Republican incumbents are sweating their reelection bids. But the GOP’s struggle to hold open seats might tell the story of the midterm elections. 

While Republican incumbents such as Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania’s 1st District and Mike Lawler of New York’s 17th have pre-established brands and extensive political networks to potentially withstand a political wave, GOP nominees in open seats don’t have the same profiles and are more at risk of losing, particularly when the storm gets rough.

While Democrats don’t need a blue wave to take control of the House – a net gain of just three seats would give them the majority – it’s helpful to look back at past cycles when a clear political tide benefited one party. 

During Trump’s first midterm, in 2018, Democrats won 12 GOP-held open House seats (and defeated 30 incumbents), according to Vital Statistics by the Brookings Institute. And Democrats picked off nine open seats in 2006 and 12 more in 2008. Republicans won 14 Democrat-held open seats in the 2010 red wave (along with knocking off 52 incumbents) so the trend doesn’t just go in one partisan direction. 

Even under a milder midterm in which Trump was more popular than he is today, Republicans would probably have struggled to hold Nebraska’s 2nd District, where GOP Rep. Don Bacon is retiring and Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump by 5 points in 2024. It also wouldn’t have been easy for Republicans to hold California 48th District, where Rep. Darrell Issa chose not to run for reelection to a redrawn seat Harris would have carried by 3 points. 

While district voters backed Trump by 3 points two years ago, Arizona’s 1st, which GOP Rep. David Schweikert vacated for an unsuccessful gubernatorial run, would have been difficult for Republicans to hold. And Michigan’s open 10th District could have still been a challenge with GOP Rep. John James running for governor. Voters here backed Trump by more than 6 points in 2024. 

Under the current political conditions, however, not only are those seats at extreme risk of a Democratic takeover, but GOP open seats in deeper-red territory are vulnerable as well. 

[The 10 most vulnerable House members just over a month before Election Day]

In Iowa, it’s not a surprise that GOP Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn are in competitive races, given the competitive nature of their respective 1st and 3rd districts. But the 2nd District, which is open due to Rep. Ashley Hinson’s Senate run, is competitive as well. Democrat Lindsay James has a significant chance of winning a seat that Trump would have carried won by 10 points. 

Republicans thought they had averted a disaster in North Carolina’s 11th District by pushing embattled Rep. Chuck Edwards out of the race. But Democrat Jamie Ager now finds himself in position to win an open seat where Trump finished ahead by 9 points in 2024. It’s not just the national political environment that’s helping Ager, but the new GOP nominee, state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom, has struggled to adapt to a high-profile national race. 

Trump carried Montana’s 1st District by more than 11 points, South Carolina’s 1st by 13 points and Florida’s 16th by 14 points – all three are competitive as well. The inclusion of retiring Rep. Vern Buchanan’s Sarasota-area seat is remarkable because Republicans thought the seat would be out of reach for Democrats under Florida’s new GOP-drawn map. But the current political climate is making the race a challenge. 

About five years ago, Democrats drew Nevada’s 2nd District to elect a Republican (in order to help the other three seats be more Democratic). But the combination of a favorable political climate and outgoing Rep. Mark Amodei’s rift with GOP nominee David Flippo is making this a real race. Trump finished ahead of Harris by 14 points here, and yet Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson has a chance. 

Trump won Kentucky’s 6th District by 15 points, but Republicans are at risk of losing the seat of Senate hopeful Andy Barr. Democrat Zach Dembo is running even or ahead of Republican nominee Ralph Alvarado in the Lexington-area district.

And some Republicans are concerned the party might lose New York Rep. Elise Stefanik’s 21st District. Trump won the North Country seat by a whopping 21 points, but public polling shows Democratic farmer Blake Gendebien running ahead of Republican sticker company CEO Anthony Constantino. While the climate is poor for Republicans across the country, it’s hard to imagine the races being this tight had Stefanik, Barr, and Amodei run for reelection.

The fact that these open seats are competitive is not unprecedented. Back in 2006, when there was an unpopular Republican president and an unpopular war in the Middle East that was driving up fuel prices, Republicans struggled to hold deep-red Idaho’s 1st District. President George W. Bush had finished ahead of Democrat John Kerry by 38 points in 2004, but Republican Bill Sali won the open seat by just 5 points two years later. Bush finished ahead of Kerry by 11 points in Wisconsin’s 8th District, and yet Democrat Steve Kagen won the open seat in 2006.

In the end, the 2024 election results might prove to be a mirage for Republicans – or just a temporary shift against Democrats – rather than a permanent realignment of the two parties. If Trump were on the ballot this November, he would struggle to match his margins from just two years ago. 

While Democrats were hurt by their open seats in 2022, when Wisconsin’s Ron Kind and New York’s Tom Suozzi, Antonio Delgado and Kathleen Rice decided not to run, the party has benefited from a relative lack of Democrat-held open seats this cycle. 

They have a few tough open seats, particularly those that were dramatically reshaped by redistricting. But Democrats are fortunate that a handful of vulnerable incumbents decided to run for reelection, even though Republican cartographers have targeted them for defeat. If Reps. Shomari Figures (Alabama’s 2nd District), Don Davis (North Carolina’s 1st), Marcy Kaptur (Ohio’s 9th), Kathy Castor (Florida’s 14th), Henry Cuellar (Texas’ 28th) and Jared Moskowitz (Florida’s 25th) had decided to call it quits in the face of challenging congressional lines, Democrats would have struggled to hold their seats, and it would have put a dent in the party’s chances for a majority.

House Democrats don’t need to win all of the GOP-held open seats to flip the chamber. But those competitive races demonstrate the nature of the cycle and help divert Republican resources to defense rather than letting the party spend on offense elsewhere.

news.title: Kamala Harris Leads Newsom in 2028 Democrat Front-Runners Poll
news.text: Former Vice President Kamala Harris has opened up a 15-point lead over California Governor Gavin Newsom in a new poll of potential Democratic presidential candidates for 2028. This is despite having yet to announce whether she will seek the White House again. The Financial Times/Focaldata survey, released on October 11, found that 30 percent of respondents considering the Democratic presidential nomination supported Harris, compared with 15 percent for Newsom. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez were tied for third place on 9 percent each, while Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff followed on 8 percent. Focaldata said its latest survey was conducted between October 2 and October 5 among 2,553 U.S. adults. The generic ballot measures which party voters would prefer to control Congress, rather than support for individual candidates in specific races. The findings come less than three weeks before the November midterm elections and amid growing speculation about who will emerge to lead the Democratic Party following GOP President Donald Trump's second term. However, the latest numbers do not represent a significant departure from previous polling; this has repeatedly placed Harris ahead of other prospective candidates. A Harvard CAPS/Harris survey conducted in late September put Harris at 38 percent and Newsom at 17 percent, while an Echelon Insights poll earlier that month found Harris leading Newsom by 24 percent to 14 percent. The new results reinforce Harris's position as an early polling front-runner while highlighting the uncertainty surrounding a presidential contest that remains more than two years away. Neither Harris nor Newsom has formally announced a 2028 presidential campaign. What Has Kamala Harris Said About Running in 2028? Harris has kept her political options open since losing the 2024 presidential election to Trump. The former vice president said in July that she had not made a decision about another White House campaign. Her position has attracted renewed scrutiny as she continues to engage with Democratic donors and support candidates ahead of the midterms. An October 6 Washington Post report described Harris as facing competing pressures within the party, with some Democrats pointing to her experience and established support base, while others question whether the party should choose a new candidate after its 2024 defeat. Harris's strong position in early primary polling also comes with a significant caveat: voters expressing a preference more than two years before an election are not necessarily committed to supporting that candidate when voting begins. Harris remains one of the most closely watched potential contenders, with her decision likely to affect the choices available to other Democrats considering a campaign. Gavin Newsom Says He Would Not Challenge Harris The new poll is particularly significant given Newsom's comments about a possible presidential contest between two of California's most prominent Democrats. In a September interview with CNN's Jake Tapper, Newsom said he would not enter the 2028 presidential race if Harris decided to run. "I wouldn't do that to her," Newsom said. "I wouldn't waste everybody's time." The governor suggested their political support overlapped considerably and questioned whether competing against Harris would serve any useful purpose. Newsom also acknowledged that he had considered running in 2024 but had not felt ready. His latest remarks leave open the possibility of a presidential campaign if Harris chooses not to enter the race. Newsom has nevertheless continued building a national profile, campaigning for Democratic candidates beyond California and positioning himself as a prominent critic of the Trump administration. His political activity has drawn attention ahead of the midterms, with several prospective 2028 candidates using the election cycle to expand their networks and test their appeal beyond their home states. What Has Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez Said? Ocasio-Cortez has also declined to rule out seeking the presidency in 2028. Asked during an August appearance on ABC's This Week whether she would consider running for president or the Senate, the New York congresswoman said she was focused on the approaching midterm elections. "I haven't ruled out the possibility," she said. Ocasio-Cortez has repeatedly emphasized that her political priorities extend beyond securing a particular office. At a University of Chicago event in May, she said: "My ambition is to change this country." The progressive Democrat has increasingly attracted national attention through her campaigning, including her support for Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. Her 9 percent showing in the latest survey places her level with Buttigieg but behind both Harris and Newsom. Other prospective Democratic candidates include Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear and Illinois Governor JB Pritzker, although none has formally secured a place in a future presidential contest. Newsweek has contacted representatives for Harris, Newsom and Ocasio-Cortez for comment via email and is awaiting responses. JD Vance Leads Republican 2028 Poll The same Financial Times/Focaldata survey also found Vice President JD Vance leading the field of potential Republican presidential candidates. Vance received 38 percent support, followed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio on 24 percent. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis was further behind on 9 percent, while Donald Trump Jr. received 7 percent. The results were broadly consistent with previous Republican primary polling. A late-September Harvard CAPS/Harris survey placed Vance at 39 percent, suggesting that his position among prospective Republican candidates has remained relatively stable. As with the Democratic contest, the numbers provide an early indication of voters' preferences rather than a definitive picture of the eventual field. Democrats Extend Midterm Polling Lead The presidential findings were released alongside polling showing Democrats holding an eight-point advantage over Republicans on the generic congressional ballot ahead of November's midterm elections. With the 2026 elections approaching, the results provide a snapshot of the broader political environment in which prospective presidential candidates are beginning to establish their national profiles. For Harris, the immediate question remains whether she will translate her continued strength in early polling into another campaign for the White House. For Newsom, her decision could be particularly consequential, given his public pledge not to challenge her for the nomination Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Tobias Meyjes and James Debens
news.summary: Kamala Harris has emerged as the leading potential Democratic presidential candidate in a new poll, ahead of Gavin Newsom.

news.title: What are the US midterms? A visual guide
news.text:
Voters in the United States on November 3rd will elect members of Congress, which is made up of two parts – the House of Representatives and the Senate.

These elections happen midway through the term of the US president – two years after the presidential elections – and determine which party controls Congress.

The outcome is important because if the president’s party does not hold a majority, it becomes difficult to pass legislation.

A key task of Congress is to create and pass federal laws – laws that apply nationwide.

The outcome will determine which political party – Donald Trump’s Republicans or opposition Democrats – controls Congress and how easy the US president can advance his agenda.

The results are also seen as a barometer of public opinion on the US president’s performance to date.

Trump’s overall approval rating has been falling for months, according to data from Real Clear Polling, down from a high of 48 per cent when he was inaugurated.

A key factor behind his successful 2024 presidential election campaign was his pledge to tackle the cost of living, posing with eggs and other household staples.

Two years on, many voters are struggling with the price of fuel, groceries, housing and healthcare. Data from the polling site Strength in Numbers shows Trump’s approval ratings have been trending in a negative direction on these issues for some time.

Who, exactly, is being elected?

All members of the House – which is the lower chamber of Congress – will be elected. The 435 representatives serve fixed terms of two years. 

To gain control of the House, a party needs a minimum of 218 seats. The Republicans hold a narrow majority after winning 219 seats in the 2024 elections. 

It will only take a few seats to flip and the power dynamics of the House will look very different.

Latest polling indicates that Democrats are likely to win the House.

In the Senate – the upper chamber of Congress – just 35 out of 100 seats are up for grabs. 

The Republicans hold 22 of these seat and Democrats 13.

To take back control of the Senate, the Democrats must flip at least four seats, including two in states where the president won by double digits. They also need to keep all of their seats.

Each of the 50 states has two senators. Office holders are elected for six-year terms on a rolling basis. Every two years, one-third of the senators come up for re-election.

Democrats are growing increasingly bullish about their chances of winning seats, even in red states such as Texas and Iowa.

What are the key states to watch?

Many seats in both chambers are not competitive because they are located in Republican or Democrat strongholds.

Most observers believe that between eight and 10 states will be competitive and could prove pivotal once the results are tallied after polls close on November 3rd. 

They include Alaska, Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas.

Keith Duggan, our Washington Correspodent, has been visiting many of these swing states. You can read his articles here.

Voting has been made more unpredictable this year because of redistricting, with several states redrawing congressional maps to swing the balance of power in House races.

Other unusual factors include Trump’s pledge to pay voters $5,000 if Republicans maintain control of Congress, as well as eye-watering sums of money being spent on campaigns in some toss-up states during the final weeks.

What do the opinion polls say? 

Since the start of 2026, most polls have given the Democrats a lead nationally.

Polling, however, has tended to understate support for Trump. In 2024, for example, most polls pointed to a Kamala Harris victory in the presidential elections. In the end, Trump won comfortably. Polls also underestimated Trump’s support when he beat Hillary Clinton in the 2016 presidential elections.

Many betting sites or, increasingly, prediction markets have been more accurate. 

According to one of the market-leaders, Polymarket, most people who have placed bets are confident that a Democratic sweep of the House and the Senate is the most likely outcome.

 How might the outcome affect Trump?

If the Democrats win either the House or the Senate then Trump will find it difficult to get laws through Congress.

While some of his domestic plans could be frustrated, the US president has found ways to exercise executive power without his wider party.

Democratic control of either chamber would mean they could use committees to investigate aspects of the Trump presidency. 

This could have knock-on effects for the Iran war, funding for Israel and Trump’s political future. Democrat control could mean investigations into the Trump administration.

If the Republicans continue to control Congress, Trump will be able to continue with his plans and policies for the remainder of his time in office.

Read more: 

Some of Keith Duggan’s latest articles on the US midterm elections:

[ Emerging Democrat star Jon Ossoff has become a chief thorn in Trump’s sideOpens in new window ]

[ Sublime evenings and empty downtowns: Democrats threaten comeback in America’s heartlandOpens in new window ]

[ Lone star Trump believes he can bend Texas and midterm elections to his willOpens in new window ]

news.title: Media narrative predicting blue wave in key battleground state not meshing with local Republicans: 'Fired up'
news.text: DAVENPORT, Iowa — As Iowa emerges as one of the most critical states in the midterm election in both House and Senate races, Fox News Digital spoke with local Republican candidates about what the media is getting right and wrong on the ground in the Hawkeye State. As local conservatives gathered at a Scott County Republican Party event near downtown Davenport in early October to watch the first gubernatorial debate, a month out from the consequential midterm election, Fox News Digital was there asking if the media narrative was accurate that Iowa was primed for a "blue wave" amid concerns about President Donald Trump’s economy, gas prices, and the war in Iran. Greg Guy, running as a Republican for treasurer in Scott County, acknowledged that Iowans are "concerned" about the price of gas, but believes they understand that the surge in cost is likely temporary after the war in Iran winds down. "Surprisingly not," Guy said when asked if he thinks a blue wave is imminent in Iowa based on the reactions he gets when he knocks on doors in the county telling voters about his campaign, which he says is focused on doing "what’s right" and "taking care" of the community. DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING. HERE ARE 3 FORCES THAT COULD STOP IT "My neighbor is one of the big people in charge of the canvassing for the Democrat Party. I don't see where they're excited to vote," Guy said. "I mean, if I talk to a hundred doors and 30 to 40% will open up, I might get one out of 40. That's a hater, and then I'll just tell them, hey, I know you're not going to vote for me, but when I'm treasurer, and you have a problem, you can still call me. They don't know what to do because they're wound up in the hate. But otherwise, I don't think there's a whole lot of belief that the Democrat Party can do anything to fix our economy." Davenport, a town of about 100,000 people in southeast Iowa along the banks of the Mississippi River, stands out as a Democratic-leaning urban pocket in an increasingly Republican Iowa. President Trump carried Scott County by roughly four points in 2024, 51% to 47%, but former Vice President Kamala Harris won Davenport’s congressional district precincts overall, reflecting the city’s more competitive and complex political profile. Trump won Iowa by about 13 points in 2024, and Republicans control the governor’s office and both chambers of the state legislature. But Scott County’s mix of urban Democrats, suburban swing voters and conservative rural communities makes it a key test of whether the GOP’s statewide strength can overcome Democratic resilience in eastern Iowa. One of the critical questions is whether conservative Iowans are frustrated enough with Republicans to vote Democrats back into power. "No, not at all," Cynthia Mensendick, a registered nurse running for election to the Iowa State Senate to represent District 49, said when asked if voters think handing Democrats control of Congress is the "right answer." "The concern is that there will be a Democrat governor because if you look at any state where a Democrat takes over, they immediately increase spending," Mensendick said, adding, "I’m not seeing that," when asked if a "blue wave" was set to occur in Iowa this November. Mensendick, who is running a campaign focused on healthcare and the high cancer rate in Iowa, says one of the top concerns with Republican voters is Iowa turning into Illinois if Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand is elected. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: THE BIGGEST SURPRISES COME AFTER OCTOBER Republicans are facing an uphill battle in Iowa, where polling shows Democrats have gained momentum in the gubernatorial, Senate and congressional races. Additionally, Republicans are going up against historical headwinds as the party in power heading into the midterms. However, Iowa has shifted more red in recent years, and the Republicans in the room in Scott County remained optimistic. Dillon Fillion, the youngest candidate in Scott County history at 22 years old, told Fox News Digital that Republicans in Iowa and nationwide have a choice between two very different parties at the end of the day. "I think people have got to weigh the options here, they either have an option of voting for socialist candidates like Abdul El-Sayed, who is a pronounced communist and supports all the things that Lenin supports, which led the Soviet Union into the downfall that it went to, or they have the support of supporting Republicans who were actually serious about cutting their taxes, which cut their taxes in 2025 with the One Big Beautiful Bill," Fillion, running for the Iowa House of Representatives in District 81, said. "And Democrats will continue to lie about that, but again, the Democrats also voted to raise their taxes 60% in 2025, voting against the Big Beautiful Bill." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Kurt Whalen isn’t running for office, but rather serves as the Scott County Iowa GOP Vice Chair, and he told Fox News Digital that while there are many frustrations with the state of affairs from Republicans in the state, he doesn’t think GOP voters will sit on the sidelines with so much at stake. "I think people are still fired up for the Republican cause. I mean, we are a big tent party. There's people that absolutely love Trump, there’s people that don’t care for him. But the reality is, Trump's been an overwhelming force for good in our country," Whalen said. "So, we can haggle about specifics, but I really think the Republican Party will ultimately come home and certainly support the president, and I would certainly encourage them to do that because what other choice do we have? I mean, the other choice is straight up, communist, Marxist, DSA, mask mandates. The Democratic Party in general, if you look at it historically, it has always been for big government against the little guy."
news.summary: Iowa Republicans in Scott County push back on "blue wave" predictions, citing voter optimism and concerns about Democratic spending ahead of midterms.

news.title: Kacey Musgraves, Kristi Noem Drama Explained as Singer Wades Into Texas Race
news.text: Country music star Kacey Musgraves and former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem have become embroiled in unexpected social media drama tied to the Texas Senate race, one of the most closely watched of the midterms cycle. Noem took to social media to pick a fight with the singer after she hosted James Talarico, the Democratic candidate, at her concert at the American Airlines Center in Dallas over the weekend. Musgraves didn’t take too kindly to Noem’s remarks. She hit back with an apparent jab at the politician’s infamous anecdote about shooting one of her own dogs. Newsweek has contacted representatives for Musgraves and Noem via emails sent outside regular business hours. The Talarico and Paxton campaigns have also been contacted for comment via email. Newsweek is awaiting responses. The feud comes against the backdrop of a competitive Senate race that could prove pivotal in deciding party control of the chamber. Democrats are seeking to flip a seat in a state that has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988. Recent polls have shown Talarico narrowly ahead. This is despite attacks from Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee, over Talarico’s nine-day absence from the campaign trail while recovering from the flu. How the Drama Started The dispute began after Talarico attended a concert by Musgraves during her "Middle of Nowhere" tour on Saturday night. Photos and videos show the Democrat was warmly received at the show. He later took to social media to thank Musgraves. "Thank you for having me last night, Kacey Musgraves!" Talarico wrote in posts on Facebook and X, alongside photos from his front row seat. This included one of the singer taking a selfie of the pair while dressed in a bedazzled top with "Dallas" written on it. Noem, the former governor of South Dakota, responded to Talarico’s post on Monday, saying she prefers Ella Langley. Noem also made a reference to the country singer's song, Choosin’ Texas, though she is from Alabama, as she endorsed Paxton. "I’ll take @ellalangleymsic over Kacey Musgraves any day. And if I’m choosin’ Texas, I’ll take Ken Paxton over James Talarico," Noem wrote. Langley has not responded to the comment, but her account has since been untagged from Noem’s post. Musgraves Fires Back Musgraves, who was born and raised in Texas, hit back at Noem with a pointed comeback. "I don't think you have a dog in this fight but if you did you would have shot it," Musgraves wrote on X. The remark appeared to be a reference to a controversial anecdote Noem included in her memoir about killing her 14-month-old dog, Cricket, whom she described as "untrainable" and "dangerous." Noem, a close ally of President Donald Trump, defended killing the dog after the revelation sparked an intense backlash, including from Republicans. At the time, she was reportedly in consideration to be Trump’s running mate in 2024. After winning a second term, Trump made Noem his Homeland Security Secretary. But the president fired her earlier this year following mounting criticism of her leadership of the Department of Homeland Security. This included her handling of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown and disaster response. Talarico: ‘Don’t Mess With Texas’ Noem has not responded to Musgraves’ jab. But Talarico shared a photo of himself with Musgraves on X on Monday night, adding: "Don’t mess with Texas." Meanwhile, Musgraves has shared a post on her Instagram that provide details about important dates for Texas voters to know. She recently angered conservatives after pausing her concert in Chicago to ask fans to donate to a nonprofit that provides legal aid to children whose parents have been deported under the Trump administration. James Talarico Vs. Ken Paxton: Latest Polls Talarico has led most polls since Paxton clinched the nomination, usually inside the margin of error. The RealClearPolitics average of polls taken from September 18 to October 8 has him leading by 2.8 points—48.1 percent to Paxton's 45.3 percent. The newest poll in that average, from the Republican-leaning Trafalgar Group, was conducted among 1,086 likely voters from October 6 to 8, largely during Talarico's absence from the campaign trail, and found him ahead 47 percent to 44 percent. A YouGov and a New York Times/Siena College poll each had him ahead by six points in early October, and a late-September Fox News poll put him two points ahead of Paxton. Paxton has polled better on the border. A Texas Pulse poll by the Texas A&M Bush School and ReconMR in late July found him ahead 48 percent to 44 percent on securing the U.S.-Mexico border. Democrats are treating Talarico's lead with caution. In interviews with Newsweek published Sunday, party strategists warned that narrow edges in Texas and other Senate races could vanish, pointing to 2024, when Kamala Harris' September lead was gone by November. "Every Democrat should be running as if they're 10 points behind," Doug Gordon, a Democratic strategist and co-founder of UpShift Strategies, told Newsweek. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Matthew Cannon and James Debens
news.summary: The ex Homeland Security secretary slammed the singer after she hosted Democratic candidate James Talarico at a Dallas concert.
news.author: Khaleda Rahman

news.title: Woman Wearing 'Release Epstein Files' Shirt Punched at Trump Rally as President Calls Her 'Scum' and Crowd Chants 'USA'
news.text: A woman wearing a 'Release the Epstein Files' shirt was punched in the face by an apparent supporter of President Donald Trump during a campaign rally in Youngstown, Ohio, on Monday, 12 October, as the president called protesters 'scum' and the crowd chanted 'USA'.The confrontation broke out at the Covelli Centre, where Trump was campaigning for Republican Senator Jon Husted ahead of November's midterm elections. The president was criticising Husted's Democratic opponent, Sherrod Brown, when a disturbance erupted in the stands. The crowd turned towards the woman, who had been heckling during the speech.Video of the rally that circulated widely on social media showed a male attendee shoving the woman to the ground, striking her in the face and pulling her by the hair. The footage appeared to show him trying to force her head towards the floor. Several officers then reached the row, took her by the collar of her jacket and steered her towards an exit.As she was led away, the woman raised her middle finger towards the crowd. The man who struck her appeared to remain inside the venue and was seen exchanging high-fives with other attendees. It was not immediately clear whether any arrests had been made.The woman was not publicly identified, and there was no confirmed information about whether she was injured or received medical treatment.Trump Tells the Heckler to 'Go on a Diet'From the stage, Trump repeatedly referred to the protester as a man and claimed the person had been paid to disrupt the event. He said the protester received money from, in his words, 'the lefties in order to destroy our country', and called such protesters 'scum'.He then turned to the protester's appearance. 'He's a fat guy, wow,' Trump said, urging the person to 'go on a diet fast'. He told the audience the protester was 'going back home to mom' and claimed that the protester's parents had voted for him.The crowd broke into chants of 'U-S-A, U-S-A' as he continued. Trump also described the demonstrator as 'a very low-class protester'.The Epstein Files Fight Behind the ShirtThe woman's shirt connected the incident to a political dispute that has followed Trump for months. The slogan referred to demands for the full release of government records on Jeffrey Epstein, the financier and convicted sex offender who died in a Manhattan jail cell in 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex-trafficking charges.Congress passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which Trump signed into law on 19 November 2025. The legislation required the Justice Department to release records relating to Epstein, subject to specified exemptions and redactions.The Justice Department said in January 2026 that it had published nearly 3.5 million pages in compliance with the law. However, the disclosures have continued to face scrutiny from Democrats and members of Trump's own party over the handling and completeness of the released material.The issue has also surfaced in the Ohio Senate race. Brown's campaign has criticised Husted over political donations from retail billionaire Les Wexner, who previously employed Epstein as his financial adviser.Wexner has not been charged with any crime related to Epstein and has denied knowledge of his criminal activities. Husted's campaign said it donated approximately $34,300 in remaining Wexner contributions to Freedom a la Cart, a nonprofit supporting survivors of human trafficking. The campaign said earlier contributions had already been spent.The Ohio Senate Race That Drew Trump to YoungstownMonday's stop was part of Trump's campaign efforts ahead of the November midterm elections. Husted is defending the Senate seat he was appointed to fill against Brown, who is trying to return to Washington after losing to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024. Trump also backed Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy during the trip.The contest has drawn national attention as Republicans seek to retain control of the Senate and Democrats attempt to gain seats in November.Trump won Ohio by approximately 11 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election. He also carried Mahoning County, where Youngstown is located, with 54.09% of the vote against Democratic nominee Kamala Harris's 44.72%.Republicans are counting on the president to encourage turnout among voters who might otherwise skip a midterm election. The midterm elections are scheduled for Tuesday, 3 November 2026.

news.title: Six, five or four? Indian Americans face an uncertain November 3
news.text:
Nine years after Democratic Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi coined the term Samosa Caucus to celebrate a record five Indian Americans serving together in Congress, there is worry. The group, which grew to six after the last elections, lost two members in the primaries earlier this year. Hope is now pinned on two new Democratic candidates benefiting from what is being called Trump fatigue.
Political forecasts give Amish Shah an edge over his Republican rival Jay Feely in Arizona's 1st Congressional District, but the race remains competitive. Forecasters range from rating it lean Democratic to calling it a toss-up, while a recent poll by Arizona-based political consulting and polling firm FirstStrategic found the two in a "statistical dead heat".
Prediction markets Polymarket and Kalshi put the probability of a Democratic victory in Arizona's 1st District at 77 per cent and 81 per cent, respectively.
Pia Dandiya, running in Florida's 22nd Congressional District, has a tougher fight on her hands. The Cook Political Report and Sabato's Crystal Ball both rate her contest against Republican Casey Askar a toss-up, while Inside Elections rates it tilt Republican. Sabato's upgraded the race from lean Republican to toss-up on October 8. Kalshi gives a Democratic victory in the district a 54 per cent chance in the latest snapshot.
Democrats hope anti-Trump sentiment will help both candidates win, but are deeply aware that both districts, though different shades of purple, voted for Trump in 2024.
There would be less anxiety surrounding Shah and Dandiya's prospects had two members of the Samosa Caucus not lost their primaries earlier this year.
Krishnamoorthi, who coined the term, decided to run for Senate after winning his Illinois 8th District seat five times in a row. He lost the Democratic Senate primary in March to Illinois Lieutenant Governor Juliana Stratton.
Democratic Rep. Shri Thanedar, whose election in 2022 had brought the number of Indian American House members to five, lost the Democratic primary in Michigan's 13th Congressional District to Donavan McKinney.
It was a stunning reversal for Indian Americans who had hoped representation would continue to grow in Washington. The caucus could return to six if both Shah and Dandiya win, remain at five if one wins, or fall to four if neither does. Democratic Reps. Ami Bera and Ro Khanna of California, Pramila Jayapal of Washington and Suhas Subramanyam of Virginia are running in districts rated solid Democratic by political forecasters, with prediction markets currently rating Democratic chances in the high 90s.
The other side of the ballot
Of course, an election is never quite over until it's over. There are three Indian American Republicans on the November ballot. Two are running against fellow Indian Americans. Ritesh Tandon faces Rep. Ro Khanna in California's 17th District, while Nirav Sheth is challenging Rep. Pramila Jayapal in Washington's 7th District. Prediction markets put the chances of a Republican victory in these districts at 3 per cent and 2 per cent, respectively.
The third Republican, Mahesh 'Max' Ganorkar, is running in North Carolina's 4th Congressional District against Democratic Rep. Valerie Foushee. The district is rated solid Democratic by forecasters. If he were to defy the forecasts and win, one more Indian American would join the House.
Three independent Indian American candidates are also running in the midterm elections. Anil Kumar, a physician, is contesting Michigan's 11th Congressional District against Democrat Jeremy Moss and Republican Ethan Baker. The district is rated solid Democratic by forecasters.
In Ohio's 13th District, independent Sandeep Dixit is challenging Democratic Rep. Emilia Sykes and Republican Carey Coleman. Forecasters rate the district likely Democratic.
In Massachusetts, Indian-born entrepreneur Shiva Ayyadurai is making a third bid for the Senate, this time as an independent against Democratic Sen. Ed Markey. In 2018, he ran against and lost to Democrat Elizabeth Warren. In 2020, he failed to win the Republican primary.
The making of the Samosa Caucus
Since its coinage in May 2017, Samosa Caucus has been used to describe the informal grouping of Indian American lawmakers in Congress, all of them Democrats. On January 10, 2025, the six Indian American members of the House issued a joint statement celebrating their record representation in the newly constituted Congress and welcoming Suhas Subramanyam as the newest member.
The term appeared in the joint statement. Jayapal said she was "thrilled that we are growing our 'Samosa Caucus' in this Congress," while Krishnamoorthi recalled, "Eight years ago, I was proud to coin the phrase 'Samosa Caucus' for our diverse and dedicated group of Indian American lawmakers in Congress".
All six pledged, in different ways, to serve Indian American communities, strengthen US-India ties and pave the way for future generations of Indian American lawmakers.
The Samosa Caucus has yet to be tested for bipartisanship. No Indian American Republican has been elected to Congress since the term was coined. The last was Bobby Jindal, who represented Louisiana in the House from 2005 to 2008.
The first Indian American elected to Congress was Dalip Singh Saund, a Democrat who won California's 29th Congressional District in 1956. He served until 1963.
It would be another 48 years before a second Indian American, Republican Bobby Jindal, was elected to the House in 2004.
After Jindal left Congress in January 2008, there was a gap of nearly five years without an Indian American in the House, until Democrat Ami Bera took office in January 2013 following his election from California in 2012.
Bera was joined in January 2017 by newly elected Democratic Sen. Kamala Harris and Democratic House members Pramila Jayapal, Ro Khanna and Raja Krishnamoorthi. Harris became the first Indian American elected to the Senate.
The Samosa Caucus has fallen to four members before. Harris resigned from the Senate to become vice president in January 2021, leaving four Indian Americans in Congress until Shri Thanedar took office in January 2023. His arrival brought the number back to five, and Suhas Subramanyam's election in 2024 took it to the much-celebrated six.
Note: All Polymarket and Kalshi probabilities cited in this article are snapshots taken at the time of writing and are subject to change.

news.title: The Top 37 Races to Watch This Midterm
news.text:
Voters’ decisions in the upcoming November midterms are set to reshape the balance of Washington and beyond. Democrats are seeking to capitalize on favorability ratings that fell below 40 percent for Republicans in the latest RealClearPolitics summary of polling.

That’s expected for the sixth year of a president’s tenure, called the “six-year itch,” a time when the president’s party has historically lost seats in the House. With the House already closely divided, observers expect Democrats to reclaim the lower chamber this year. However, Democrats’ new margins in the House could also be slim, as a flurry of mid-decade redistricting has panned out with a slight edge for Republicans.

Here are the top elections and candidates to watch this cycle.

In Georgia, Republicans are again seeking to flip one of the state’s two Senate seats, which have been held by Democrats since 2020.

Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), elected to his first six-year term in a January 2021 runoff, is up for reelection. Republicans selected Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.) to take him on.

In 2024, President Donald Trump won Georgia by around 2.2 percentage points— Republicans’ lowest margins of victory in the Peach State since 1996.

In Maine, incumbent Sen. Susan Collins (R-Me.) will take on former state Senate President Troy Jackson for one of the year’s top Senate fights.

Collins, a long-serving political juggernaut in the state, ran unopposed for her party’s nomination.

Maine Democrats selected Jackson on July 25 as their party’s nominee to challenge Collins, taking over after the previous nominee, Graham Platner dropped out of the race.

Platner, a progressive, was one of the first candidates to capture the populist mood of the national Democratic base, building a campaign that championed pro-working class policies. But after accusations of sexual and other misconduct emerged, which he denied, Platner ultimately departed the race.

However, Collins still faces a difficult fight to hold the seat, with polls showing she’s running behind either Democrat in most polls conducted since March.

Michigan’s Senate race features a showdown between an establishment Republican and a progressive outsider after Democratic Sen. Gary Peters declined to run for reelection.

El-Sayed will take on former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in the race.

Currently, he leads in the polls by around 4 percent.

Analysts say El-Sayed’s campaign reflects the outsider approach and populist energy seen among democratic socialist-aligned candidates.

Between 2017 and 2020, El-Sayed spoke at several events hosted by the Democratic Socialists of America.

But today, El-Sayed says he’s distanced himself from the group—and the democratic socialist label—describing himself as a capitalist.

Rogers ran unopposed during his primary with Trump’s endorsement.

While Alaska is Republican-leaning, the Senate race between incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola is proving competitive.

Sullivan has served in the Senate since 2015, while Peltola served in the U.S. House of Representatives between September 2022 and January 2025.

Because Peltola has shown viability in statewide elections in the single-district state, the Last Frontier is a top target for Democrats this year.

The ranked-choice race is complicated by the presence of a candidate on the ballot who shares a name with incumbent senator Dan Sullivan. The challenger, also named Dan Sullivan and also Republican, has insisted he’s serious about running, despite allegations that he’s just trying to divert votes away from the senator.

In the most recent poll taken of the race, Sullivan leads with 47 percent to Peltola’s 46 percent. However, some other polls show Peltola in the lead.

Iowa is also home to a competitive Senate race this year, this time between GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek, after Sen. Joni Ernst declined to run for a third term.

Like others, the state had been seen as reliably Republican over the past several cycles, since President Donald Trump first won the state back in 2016 with a nearly 10-point victory.

However, it was long known as a quintessential swing state.

As recently as 2012, the state drew intense national attention as a battleground. Now, some polls are showing that Iowa is in for a tighter Senate race this year, a pattern also being seen in neighboring Ohio.

Hinson has led in five polls conducted of the race since April, while Turek has led in four.

Cook Political Report recently moved the race from lean Republican to a toss up, reflecting the closely split nature of the race.

Ohio is another key Senate battleground this year, with former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown set for a November fight against incumbent GOP Sen. Jon Husted.

Brown was unseated just two years ago in the 2024 election, losing to Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) by around 3.6 percent—far outrunning Trump and Vice President JD Vance’s approximately 11 point victory that year.

Without the benefit of the “Trump effect,” describing Trump’s impact on close down-ballot races during presidential election years, Husted faces a race against a politically powerful opponent with deep name recognition in the state.

Husted was appointed by Gov. Mike DeWine to fill the seat held by Vance. The winner will serve out the final two years of Vance’s term.

In Texas, state Attorney General Ken Paxton is set for a heated November matchup against Democratic state Rep. James Talarico in one of the cycle’s most-watched races.

Paxton won a contentious primary against incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) with the assistance of a strong endorsement from Trump.

The expensive and personal primary race centered heavily on Paxton’s past controversies, including his impeachment for alleged bribery, whistleblower retaliation, and abuse of office.

In 2023, Paxton was impeached by the Texas House on 20 articles in a 121–23 vote and subsequently acquitted on all counts.

Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian, has built a campaign based around his Christian values as a seminarian and on his track record as a state legislator.

Talarico has led in 15 out of the 16 polls of the race conducted since July, with Paxton leading in a poll conducted by Emerson College.

In North Carolina, former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley is set to take on former Gov. Roy Cooper in one of the 2026 cycle’s most crucial matchups.

Trump has loomed over the election in the state.

Whatley, appointed to lead the Republican National Committee on Trump’s recommendation, has emphasized his loyalty, while Cooper has accused Whatley of being “anointed” by Trump.

In Kansas, polls show Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas) locked in a dead heat with pastor Adam Hamilton.

Hamilton is a United Methodist megachurch pastor and author, co-founding the Kansas-based Church of the Resurrection. Marshall is a freshman senator and an obstetrician-gynecologist, first elected in 2020 after beating out a crowded primary field.

This year, Marshall has been the subject of controversy in the state after The New York Times reported that he had sued hundreds of his former patients, leading to 81 arrests due to missed court dates.

While Marshall led in the first poll taken of the race released on Sept. 11, every poll since has shown him either tied with or running behind Hamilton.

In the 2020 election, which he won by around 12 percent, there were some warning signs: Shawnee County and Riley County backed the Democrat for the first time since the 1970s, while Johnson County voted Democratic for the first time in the state’s history. President Joe Biden flipped the same counties in that election.

The race was originally rated lean Republican by Cook Political Report, which now rates it to be a toss-up.

In Nebraska, independent candidate Dan Osborn—who made national news following his close fight against Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) in 2024—is making another bid for the office.

In that race, Osborn lost to Fischer by around 7 points after Democrats declined to make a nomination in the race. This year, Democratic nominee Cindy Burbank has dropped out of the race to make way for Osborn, similar to the situation seen in 2024.

This year, he’s running against the incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), and polls have shown a tight race. In surveys taken in September and October, Ricketts led by 4 and 5 points, respectively. Osborn led by around the same margin in polls taken in May and September.

Republicans maintain a structural advantage in the state. Although 53 percent of registered Nebraska voters live in rural areas, the urban and suburban population in Nebraska is reliably Republican—but has potential to swing in line with an anti-Republican national environment.

Omaha, Nebraska, is a crucial decision-maker in the race, as its population has trended away from Republicans in recent cycles, voting for Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024.

In Texas’ 34th Congressional District, representing one of the Lone Star State’s most evenly-split seats, incumbent Rep. Vicente Gonzalez (D-Texas) is seeking to hold off a challenge from Republicans, who see the House district as a potential pickup opportunity.

In the primary, Trump-endorsed candidate Eric Flores, a former federal prosecutor, defeated former Rep. Mayra Flores (R-Texas) for the Republican nod.

In 2022, Mayra Flores made headlines with a special election win in District 34 before its map was redrawn. But after she lost to Gonzalez in 2022 and again in 2024, the party is making a fresh bid with Eric Flores.

The Cook Political Report rates the race a toss-up.

The district was altered to favor Republicans, although analysts still consider the seat competitive.

Davis won a second term in 2024 by less than 2 percent, becoming one of 13 House Democrats to win elections in districts won by Trump. He’s been critical of the redrawing of his district, which will make reelection a tougher challenge this cycle.

With the House already closely divided, observers expect Democrats to reclaim the lower chamber this year. Collins, a long-serving political juggernaut in the state, ran unopposed for her party’s nomination.

However, Collins still faces a difficult fight to hold the seat, with polls showing she’s running behind either Democrat in most polls conducted since March.

Rogers ran unopposed during his primary with Trump’s endorsement.

news.title: Trump says 'would love' to serve third term as US president
news.text:
WASHINGTON, October 13. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump said he would like to run for a third term as US president if he had the opportunity.

"I would love to do that," the Associated Press quoted him as saying while addressing Republican Party supporters in Ohio ahead of the November US congressional elections as the crown broke into chants of "four more years."

By law, Trump’s second term as president is set to end in January 2029. The 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution, which was adopted in 1951, limits a president’s tenure to two terms. Nevertheless, the current US leader has repeatedly indicated the possibility of seeking re-election for a third term. Steve Bannon, the president’s former key political strategist, also insisted last fall that Trump be president again.

Trump won the election for the second time in November 2024. He defeated Democratic Party candidate Kamala Harris. He previously headed the US administration from 2017 to 2021.

news.title: MAGA News Channel Cuts Away as Interview Goes Off the Rails
news.text:
A right-wing channel abruptly cut away from an interview with a Donald Trump rallygoer after the segment quickly derailed.

During coverage of Trump’s rally in Youngstown, Ohio on Monday, Real America’s Voice cut to Bobby McNeily, a reporter for the Pro-Trump network. McNeily, who was inside the arena, introduced an interview with a man he spoke with earlier while he was waiting in line. The man was identified as Brian. 

McNeily opened by riffing on Brian’s Forrest Gump T-shirt, quoting the movie’s “I just felt like running” line and adding, “I love that movie.” Then the bit fell apart. 

Looking baffled, McNeily told viewers he was “hearing from friends” that the man beside him was “not a fan of President Trump.” 

“It’s very interesting,” McNeily said, “because I’ve never really spoken to anyone that I can recall, interviewing them, not a fan of President Trump, but standing in line to see him. Brian then revealed that it was his first Trump rally.

“What are you hoping to hear tonight?” McNeily asked. 

“What I hope to hear is not what I plan to hear… what I plan to hear is a bunch of rhetoric, a bunch of lies, a bunch of the same old script, that sort of stuff,” Brian said. 

“I’m here to get a firsthand perspective of the kind of lies and garbage and stuff that he’s going to probably be peddling for the next two years, as if the first two haven’t been bad enough.”

“Do you consider yourself a registered Democrat, or how would you vote before?” McNeily asked. 

“I was independent, because I consider myself moderate,” he said. 

“I was independent until JD Vance entered our ballot, and then I actually registered for a Republican. My strategy being, if I can keep him off the general election ballot by voting against him in a primary, then I get two chances to eliminate all these MAGA idiots. That’s my approach.” 

McNeily then followed up with a question about whether Vance’s selection had encouraged him.

“Oh, I can’t stand him,” Brian said. “I mean, it’s basically anybody that endorses or is endorsed by Donald is not a fan of mine.”

Moments later, the interview cut away from Brian mid-sentence. The network then cut back to a studio panel, including McNeily, who were asked for a “quick reaction.”

Host Grant Stinchfield marveled at how politely he thought Brian had been treated. 

“The left would not be as nice to us if we were at a, God forbid, Kamala Harris rally,” he said. “But he’s Trump-deranged, isn’t he?”

“Absolutely, Grant,” McNeily replied. Still, he said he was “holding out hope” for Brian. “I’m an optimistic guy.”

McNeily guessed that Brian had “listened to crazy far left outlets instead of actually really seeking the truth in all of this.”

The rally came three weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. 

Trump was in Youngstown to campaign for Sen. Jon Husted, 59. The Republican was appointed to Vance’s old seat in 2025, after Vance became vice president. Husted is trailing former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown as the GOP fights to hold onto a state Trump won by double digits in 2024, according to the Hill. 

Trump’s swing through Ohio comes as his approval ratings hit historic lows. A Pew Research Center poll released last week found that only three in ten Americans now approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president.

The Daily Beast has reached out to the White House and Real America’s Voice for comment.
news.summary:
RAVA right-wing channel abruptly cut away from an interview with a Donald Trump rallygoer after the segment quickly derailed.

During coverage of Trump’s rally in Youngstown, Ohio on Monday, Real America’s Voice cut to Bobby McNeily, a reporter for the Pro-Trump network. McNeily, who was inside the arena, introduced an interview with a man he spoke with earlier while he was waiting in line. The man was identified as Brian. 

McNeily opened by riffing on Brian’s Forrest Gump T-shirt, quoting the movie’s “I just felt like running” line and adding, “I love that movie.” Then the bit fell apart.

news.title: Musk spends $276 mn on midterms to help Republicans retain Congress control
news.text: Elon Musk has spent roughly $366 million ​in the 2026 US midterm election cycle so far, $276 million of it since July to help Republicans retain control of Congress, even as Democrats' chances of retaking the US House and Senate have improved. Musk's largess, which was reported earlier by the New York Times, makes the world's richest person likely the single-biggest political donor in this year's races, according to campaign finance ‌records. There is a lot at stake for Musk with ​Democrats in the US House of Representatives ​calling for investigations into his government contracts as CEO of aerospace company SpaceX as well as his work ​running the Department of Government Efficiency under President Donald Trump. Here is a breakdown of his political spending, which was confirmed by a spokesman for his super PAC America PAC. Musk has spent $366 million so far this election cycle, which began January 1, 2025. At least $276 million so far has gone to Republican groups and ​his own super PAC since July. Of the $276 million in third-quarter donations: $158 million went to the Senate Leadership Fund, ‌the super PAC set up to help elect Republicans to the Senate that is aligned with Senate ​Majority Leader John Thune, a Republican from South Dakota. $20 million went to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the super PAC set up for House Republicans that is aligned with House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican. $76 million went to Musk's America ‌PAC. $10 million went to the Lone Star ​Liberty PAC, which is supporting Republican state Attorney General ‌Ken Paxton's run for the US Senate in Texas, where recent polls have him in a dead ‌heat against Democrat James Talarico. $10 million went to the Republican Governors Association. $2 million went to the Republican ​Attorneys General Association. America PAC is helping Republican candidates in seven battleground states and nearly three dozen House races. The new giving will be publicly disclosed when many ​super PACs are required to disclose their third-quarter spending on Thursday. Musk has also donated more money through groups that do not disclose their donors, according to the New York Times report. Roughly $90 million spent this cycle paid for work done in the prior election or supported other issues, including ‌an unsuccessful candidate for the Wisconsin Supreme Court and a controversial program paying $1 million to registered voters who signed a petition supporting free speech and gun rights, according to an America PAC spokesman. Musk spent roughly $290 million during the last election cycle in which Trump won the presidential election race against former Vice President Kamala Harris.

news.title: Trump repeatedly attacks Minnesota, Omar during Ohio campaign stop
news.text:

He accused Democrats in Minnesota of cheating in the elections, saying he thought he won the state in 2024 before “a rather large drop of votes” showed up. Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris won Minnesota in 2024.

“The once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants. There is Violence, Murder, and Mayhem all over the State,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “The people of Minnesota must fight back.”
