news.title: Senate ratings change: Kansas and Minnesota tighten
news.text:
With three weeks to go until Election Day, the Senate battlefield is getting bigger. MS NOW is moving Kansas to “lean Republican” and Minnesota to “lean Democratic,” pulling two seats that once looked more secure into competitive territory.

Kansas joined our list of races to watch last month, when we categorized it as “likely Republican.” While we still give the GOP the edge in defending this seat, several factors have moved it into a more competitive category: lean Republican.

For one, polling continues to show Democrat Adam Hamilton neck and neck with incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall. As we explained a few weeks ago, the national environment looks bleak enough for the GOP that even a state as red as Kansas could be decided by single digits this year. Hamilton, a well-known United Methodist pastor, appears to be a strong nominee, while Marshall has been fending off questions about his past medical billing practices and, as MS NOW recently reported, his campaign finances. Even so, it is striking that polls have shown Hamilton tied or even slightly ahead of Marshall in a state Trump won by 16 points.

The polls do warrant some caution, however. Voters who backed Trump in 2024 are more likely to be undecided than those who supported Kamala Harris — a pattern visible in recent New York Times/Siena and YouGov polls. If those undecided voters ultimately break toward Marshall, in line with their past votes, he has room to gain a few points.

The polls also show a fair amount of ticket-splitting, with Republican gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson running ahead of Marshall. But the bigger question is how many voters will actually back a Republican for governor and Democrat for Senate in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century. And while midterm polling has been fairly accurate on average in recent cycles, polls in individual states often miss by several points. It is not hard to imagine that pollsters are once again struggling to reach reliably Republican voters.

Voter registration trends offer Democrats another somewhat encouraging sign. Statewide, registered Republicans outnumber registered Democrats, 45% to 26%. But recent months have suggested some energy on the Democratic side: Democrats outpaced Republicans in new registrations by a 2-to-1 margin in August and September, according to the Kansas Secretary of State’s office. While the new registrants are just a drop in the bucket compared to Republicans’ overall advantage, it is a markedly different pattern than in 2022, when Republicans outpaced Democrats during the same period. Kansas also has a sizable pool of unaffiliated voters, who are likely to play a big role in determining the final margin. Polls suggest they favor Hamilton.

Finally, Republicans and their affiliated groups are acting like Kansas is truly competitive. Vice President JD Vance visited the state last month to rally support, and the Senate Leadership Fund PAC started spending big on this race in late September. It now has more than $10 million in ad time reserved, according to AdImpact. That may reflect an abundance of caution, since wave elections often bring surprise upsets that benefit the party out of power. Either way, it is remarkable that Republicans feel the need to shore up support in a seat like this one at all.

On paper, Minnesota should be an easy hold for Democrats in the current environment: It has not elected a Republican senator in more than 20 years, and it has not voted Republican for president in more than 50. It is also a must-win for Democrats hoping to retake the Senate majority. But polling has consistently shown this open-seat race within reach for Republicans. That is the main reason we are moving it from “likely Democratic” to “lean Democratic.”

With Sen. Tina Smith retiring, Democrats have no incumbency advantage here. If anything, there might be a bit of a disadvantage being linked to Democratic leadership in the state. Progressive Lt Gov. Peggy Flanagan won the party’s August primary over centrist Rep. Angie Craig. But it is also possible that the state’s social services scandal, which has cost Gov. Tim Walz politically, could also pose a challenge, and Flanagan may struggle to distance herself from it. Republican nominee Michele Tafoya, a well-known former NFL reporter, has been hammering Flanagan over the issue.

There has not been much polling in this race, but what little there is shows a close contest. Flanagan leads Tafoya by about four points, on average — the same modest margin by which Harris won the state in 2024. The country has clearly shifted to the left since then.

On top of nationwide economic discontent, Minnesota has seen social unrest and violence involving federal agents following the Trump administration’s deployment of Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to the state. Those developments have meant an even stronger leftward swing. Instead, polls suggest a more muted shift. The same polls show Flanagan running a few points behind Sen. Amy Klobuchar, the Democratic gubernatorial nominee, who looks likely to succeed Walz.

We do not know precisely how polls will err this year. Is it possible they are understating Democratic strength in Minnesota, while overstating it in Kansas? Absolutely, but we will not know until Election Day. That is why we treat polling as an informative signal, but not the final word. Both states could be competitive this year, but their recent electoral history gives the incumbent party a baseline advantage we cannot ignore.

news.title: Democrats have knives out for John Fetterman — but risk stabbing themselves
news.text:
“I’d love to see him as a Republican,” President Donald Trump told reporters Saturday.

He was speaking, of course, of Sen. John Fetterman, the maverick Pennsylvania Democrat who’s been increasingly willing to break with his party in recent months.

Trump’s comment revved up a rumor mill that Fetterman himself recently sought to tamp down.

“I don’t have a reason” to jump ship to the Republicans, he assured CBS’ Major Garret two weeks ago. 

Then he dropped a quiet bombshell. 

“If I’m 51” — that is, the Senate’s 51st Democrat and the deciding vote for the body’s control — “then I don’t know.”

Fetterman has every reason to be coy — it makes him Washington’s most powerful kingmaker.

But more importantly, a Fetterman exit would be an ominous signal of coming attractions for his party. 

In 2024, the Democratic Party politburo lied about President Joe Biden’s fitness for a second term, then about Kamala Harris’ readiness for prime time.

Former President Barack Obama has swooned for Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, a candidate who can’t condemn the Muslim Brotherhood and refuses to say that the Nazi leadership in Tehran “is a greater threat” than the multiracial democracy in Israel. 

New York Mayor Zoran Mandami blames Israeli Jews for the genocidal Oct. 7attack, while his wife boosts social posts celebrating that barbarism.

But half of House Democrats have already voted to cut off Israel aid — and with Democrats like New Jersey’s Adam Hamawy soon heading for Congress, the trend line is clear. 

If Fetterman does leave, the impact could be enormous.

He reflects the values of not just the anti-terror centrists, but of a broad swath of working-class voters who share his stances on immigration, gender, crime, race and so much else.

Fetterman already enjoys a 77% approval rating among Pennsylvania Republicans and 48% approval statewide.

Regardless of what happens on Nov. 3, that toxic brand bodes poorly for 2028 and beyond. 

The Pennsylvania maverick clearly senses that moderates are no longer welcome in his party.

If he bails out after November, the question will be how many of us he takes with him.

news.title: Report: Kamala Harris ‘Lays Groundwork’ for 2028 Campaign
news.text:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris is laying the groundwork for a third presidential campaign, speaking with major donors, hiring staff, and traveling to battleground states, according to a Wall Street Journal report.

The former vice president has told associates she remains undecided on another White House run, but she has taken steps that could precede a 2028 bid, the Journal reported, citing multiple people familiar with the conversations.

Harris has publicly tied her plans to the November midterms, telling a NAACP event in Michigan last month that the next cycle depends on this one.

“I have not decided if I’m going to run again,” Harris said, drawing a lengthy standing ovation. “I do sincerely believe ‘28 won’t matter if we don’t get through ‘26.”

The former Democrat nominee has appeared at a half-dozen private California fundraisers ahead of the midterms and joined a Democratic National Committee get-out-the-vote call urging more than 2,000 volunteers to knock on doors across a dozen states. She has also assembled a team of advisers, including chief of staff Candace Bond, a former ambassador to Trinidad and Tobago, and communications director Eduardo Negrón.

The Harris Victory Fund raised more than $10.3 million between January and September 2025, with $8.5 million of that coming from contributions under $200, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings.

Not everyone in her orbit is convinced. Some donors have told Harris directly that a bid would be a long shot, the Journal reported, and her husband, Doug Emhoff, has privately told people he would prefer she not run, though those close to him expect he would support a campaign.

The skepticism extends to her 2024 financial base. The Los Angeles Times contacted more than two dozen top donors to the largest pro-Harris super PAC in May, many of whom gave at least $1 million, and found little appetite for a repeat.

“I think it is too early to pick a favorite in the 2028 race, but Kamala Harris will not be my candidate,” one donor said.

Harris still leads most hypothetical 2028 Democrat primary polls and retains strong support among black voters. California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), another potential contender, said in a September CNN interview he would not run if Harris entered, calling a two-Californian primary a “gift from God for everybody else.”

The possible bid comes after a 2024 cycle in which Harris secured the nomination without an open primary following President Joe Biden’s abrupt exit, then lost the Electoral College and popular vote to President Donald Trump. Harris first signaled her openness to another run in April, telling the Rev. Al Sharpton’s National Action Network convention she “might” enter the race.
news.summary:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris is laying the groundwork for a third presidential campaign, speaking with major donors, hiring staff, and traveling to battleground states.
